During and after the coronavirus pandemic, it appeared that 10-20% of the people who got infected with the COVID-19 virus developed long-term complaints (World Health Organization, 2022).
This is called Long COVID, and worldwide, at least 65 million people have or had this condition, a number that is still increasing1 (Davis et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This is called Long COVID, and worldwide, at least 65 million people have or had this condition, a number that is still increasing1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Davis et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A new health pandemic is born.
The daily lives of people with Long COVID are impacted because of impaired physical, cognitive, and/or social functions (Brus et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The daily lives of people with Long COVID are impacted because of impaired physical, cognitive, and/or social functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brus et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although most people infected with the coronavirus are only affected a little and recover within months, there remains a group of people who develop severe and systematic symptoms for a much longer period of time (O'Connor et al., 2024; Office for National Statistics, 2023).

text.text: Their abilities to e.g., work, go to school, socialize, care for themselves, and do physical exercise are affected severely (Brus et al., 2024).

text.text: This group of people needs to actively adjust their lives to survive the day and execute everyday tasks.

Currently, in the Netherlands, approximately 90,000 people have severe Long COVID (Dankers et al., 2023; Ministerie van Sociale Zaken en Werkgelegenheid,2023; Office for National Statistics, 2023) 2 and even more people are limited in their regular daily living (having milder Long COVID than the socalled 'severe cases').

text.text: Thus, the impact of Long COVID on the quality of life is enormous for many people.

This, of course, also impacts society; Long COVID leads to high societal costs as a consequence of decrease in productivity, incapacity to work, costs of care (not only acute care but also long-term care like home care), loss of children and young people in education, decreasing participation of people in other areas like informal care (Brus et al., 2024; Maatschappelijk Impact Team, 2023a).

text.text: More and more research on self-management methods and assistive tools is being done.
However, these studies mostly include physical-focused treatment interventions or technologies.
This is a limited view of how one can manage and implement strategies in one's everyday life; daily activities include a lot of cognitive functioning.
As Long COVID often impairs the (executive) cognitive functions, it is valuable to look deeper into how these can be supported (Davis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As Long COVID often impairs the (executive) cognitive functions, it is valuable to look deeper into how these can be supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This thesis aims to contribute to more insight into how people with life-limiting Long COVID can be supported in the cognitive aspects of their everyday lives using a human-centered, qualitative approach focusing on the use of technology as assistance Therefore, this study investigates the current role of technology in facilitating cognitive functioning in everyday life with Long COVID and explores how technology can be designed or adapted to improve this cognitive support in the future.
The corresponding research question is "What is the (potential) role of technology in the management of cognitive aspects of everyday life of people with Long COVID?"
To answer the main research question, the impact of Long COVID on everyday lives and the implementation of cognitive strategies and supporting technologies need to be established first.

Therefore, the following sub-research questions are answered first: RQ1: "How does Long COVID affect the everyday lives of people who experience fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and eventual Post Exertional Malaise-related symptoms that reduce their ability to carry out day-to-day activities severely?"

and RQ2: "How do people with Long COVID-related fatigue and cognitive dysfunction adjust and implement cognitive strategies and technology in order to manage the cognitive aspects their everyday life?".

Additionally, the potential and ideas of the lives experience experts need to be identified as well, which is done by answering the following question: RQ3: "What do people with Long COVID currently miss in their developed strategies and implemented technological supporting tools to carry-out daily cognition-involved activities and what can be improved?".

text.text: Long COVID 3 is an illness that can develop after a SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infection, leading to impairments in physical, cognitive, and/or social functioning.
There are multiple definitions and names to describe this condition (Munblit et al., 2022; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024).
text.formatted: There are multiple definitions and names to describe this condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Munblit et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This thesis follows the definition and notation of the World Health Organization (WHO) that is adopted by many research projects and governmental institutions in, among others, the Netherlands and the European Union.

The WHO defines Long COVID as "the continuation or development of new symptoms 3 months after the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, with these symptoms lasting for at least 2 months with no other explanation" (World Health Organization, 2022).
text.formatted: The WHO defines Long COVID as "the continuation or development of new symptoms 3 months after the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, with these symptoms lasting for at least 2 months with no other explanation" <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Long COVID can affect all infected people regardless of age, health, disability, socioeconomic status, gender, ethnicity, and living situation.
These factors can however influence the severity and manifestation of the condition (Atchison et al., 2023; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024).
text.formatted: These factors can however influence the severity and manifestation of the condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Atchison et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: To understand the impact of Long COVID on people's lives, it is important to get some more insight into its manifestation and its complex workings.
Long COVID can manifest in single or multiple symptoms and single or multiple diagnosable conditions (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024).
text.formatted: Long COVID can manifest in single or multiple symptoms and single or multiple diagnosable conditions <ref type="bibr">(National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A prominent study led by people with Long COVID showed that there are more than 200 symptoms that people can experience long after their COVID-19 infection, with fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and Post-Exertional Malaise (PEM) as the most common ones (Davis et al., 2021).

text.text: The symptoms can be categorized into ten categories, like systemic, musculoskeletal, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (Davis et al., 2021).

text.text: Long COVID is seen as a complex condition that is difficult to recover from, as multiple (organ) systems within the body are involved (Medinger & Altmann, 2022; Perumal et al., 2023).

text.text: In practice, this leads to individuals who often suffer from multiple symptoms in variable compositions with differing severity and duration, leading to divergent disease profiles (Medinger & Altmann, 2022).

text.text: For example, while some individuals lose their sense of smell and taste for a few months, others suffer from long-term systemic fatigue, severe brain fog, and worsening symptoms after (minimal) exertion for years.
Another consequence of this is that symptoms are often closely connected, which makes it even more complicated for people with Long COVID to execute everyday tasks.
Although the exact underlying systems are difficult to identify, it seems that Long COVID shares similar grounds with other conditions regarding mechanisms and symptoms.

Long COVID is associated with other (chronic) conditions like ME/CFS (Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue 3 Because of the short existence of the disease, research about this condition is currently in full development.

text.text: Besides, people with Long COVID can develop other conditions like diabetes or dysautonomia (Appelman et al, 2024; Dorronzoro-Zubiete et al, 2024; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine et al., 2024).

text.text: These conditions are also seen as complex; for many of them, no effective treatment has been found yet.
Because of the similar nature, this study's methodological approach and findings could be beneficial for insights about the management of these related (semi-)chronic conditions as well.
In this thesis, the focus will be on people with Long COVID who are less capable of executing day-today tasks than before they had Long COVID, and experience persistent symptoms.
This includes people with severe Long COVID, but also people who have less severe Long COVID but are still considerably limited in their everyday lives.
This group of people needs to make adjustments in their lives to survive the day and execute (cognitive) daily tasks.
As this thesis investigates supporting cognitive functioning in everyday life, it is important to understand the symptoms that actively contribute to impaired cognitive (executive) functioning.
First of all, the main symptom of difficulties in executing cognition-involved tasks; cognitive dysfunction.

Cognitive dysfunction due to Long COVID affects operational processes and abilities of the brain. Zhao et al. (2024) indeed observed that a direct (objective) consequence of cognitive dysfunction is a lower cognitive processing speed.

text.text: However, the exact manifestation of cognitive dysfunction due to Long COVID occurs in different combinations.
In the leading symptoms list of Davis et al. (2021), cognitive complaints are mainly embodied by 1) brain fog, 2) memory issues, and 3) speech and language issues.
text.formatted: In the leading symptoms list of <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davis et al. (2021)</ref>, cognitive complaints are mainly embodied by 1) brain fog, 2) memory issues, and 3) speech and language issues.

text.text: Brain fog is characterized by confusion, short-term memory loss, dizziness, and inability to concentrate, leading to a feeling of cloudiness in one's cognitive awareness (Garg et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Brain fog is characterized by confusion, short-term memory loss, dizziness, and inability to concentrate, leading to a feeling of cloudiness in one's cognitive awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Garg et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Further, memory issues can manifest in short-and long-term memory loss, but also in, for example, the inability to make new memories.
Speech and language problems, on the other hand, occur through difficulties finding the right words, communicating verbally, processing text, etc. (Davis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Speech and language problems, on the other hand, occur through difficulties finding the right words, communicating verbally, processing text, etc. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, cognitive dysfunction affects the ability to execute activities in everyday life; daily tasks like work, decision-making, or cooking get complicated and sometimes even impossible to perform for people with Long COVID (Davis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As a result, cognitive dysfunction affects the ability to execute activities in everyday life; daily tasks like work, decision-making, or cooking get complicated and sometimes even impossible to perform for people with Long COVID <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive dysfunction and its manifestation in everyday life are highly associated with fatigue (Davis et al., 2021; Gloeckl et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Cognitive dysfunction and its manifestation in everyday life are highly associated with fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gloeckl et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Fatigue in Long COVID is a different experience than 'usual' tiredness; people with Long COVID characterize this fatigue as a systemic exhaustion in every physical and cognitive part of the body (Medinger & Altmann, 2022).
text.formatted: Fatigue in Long COVID is a different experience than 'usual' tiredness; people with Long COVID characterize this fatigue as a systemic exhaustion in every physical and cognitive part of the body <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Medinger & Altmann, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In conversations with people with Long COVID by journalist Ed Yong, the fatigue was described as completely draining, which results in substantial life changes influencing people's capabilities, social contact, and (mental) well-being (Yong, 2023).

text.text: Many people with Long COVID are permanently tired.
This means that they wake up fatigued and get more exhausted when their energy battery becomes emptier during the day.
Fatigue has a major impact on cognitive functioning.
Therefore, it is seen as the leading symptom for difficulties in cognition-involved everyday tasks, together with cognitive dysfunction.

Lastly, Post-Exertional Malaise (PEM) is also a common symptom that burdens everyday life, and on the other hand, is associated with the severity of symptoms and (cognitive) functioning (Appelman et al., 2024; Davis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Lastly, Post-Exertional Malaise (PEM) is also a common symptom that burdens everyday life, and on the other hand, is associated with the severity of symptoms and (cognitive) functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Appelman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note that it is not always associated with cognitive dysfunction, but it has a massive impact on how people manage and deal with their Long COVID and severely affects the ability to execute everyday tasks.
Therefore, it will be actively considered in this study and the accompanying method.
PEM means that after excessive exercise that does not fit within the limited exercise capacity of their bodies, symptoms worsen or relapse.

As a result, people with Long COVID who have PEM-related complaints should monitor the boundaries of their condition so their illness will not become worse (Appelman et al., 2024; Davis et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As a result, people with Long COVID who have PEM-related complaints should monitor the boundaries of their condition so their illness will not become worse <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Appelman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davis et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Triggers could be cognitive exercise, but also physical and social activities; everything that takes effort is a trigger.
PEM complicates the rehabilitation and recovery process and limits the lives of people with Long COVID even more.
PEM is also often associated with ME/CFS (Gloeckl et al., 2023).
text.formatted: PEM is also often associated with ME/CFS <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gloeckl et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: An example of how PEM works is that cognitive fatigue relates to physical fatigue and pain, meaning that one can feel physically tired or develop pain in their muscles after cognitive effort.
You could say that PEM is the worst-case manifestation of the underlying connections and involvement of multiple (organ) systems in the body; it amplifies the complexity of living with Long COVID.
Taken together, people with Long COVID who suffer from fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and/or PEM need to do a cost-benefit analysis for every activity.
Even the simplest day-to-day tasks like showering or cooking can be a great burden as they include physical strength but also ask for cognitive resources to execute all the involved steps.

text.text: To get insight into how technology currently and potentially plays a role in managing the cognitive aspects of everyday life, it is important to get a better understanding of current findings on how one can manage health-related complaints in everyday life.

Therefore, we will look into the literature about self-management methods, how this is applied in the context of Long COVID, and the implementation of technology and other cognitive artifacts to manage complaints and cognitive activities.
Currently, there is no proven, working medical remedy against Long COVID.
Although there is a wide range of treatment methods for Long COVID, most of them were tested among a too small or uncontrolled sample.
Besides, they apply different underlying pathophysiologic bases (Bonilla et al., 2023; Fox et al., 2023).

text.text: They say that to be effective, people need to be able to understand the manifestation of their condition and apply cognitive, behavioral, and emotional measures to keep a decent quality of life.
This means that one needs to be actively involved in the development of their symptom and controlling the adjustments of their lives and the (psychosocial) impact on their life (Newman et al., 2004).

text.text: Selfmanagement methods can be applied through, e.g., (cognitive) strategies, adjustments in life standards, and the use of (cognitive) artifacts.

People with Long COVID who experience fatigue and cognitive dysfunction (and potential PEMrelated symptoms) benefit from self-management methods that focus on reducing (cognitive) load and executing day-to-day activities that involve cognitive functioning.
This can be done by managing so-called 'cognitive strategies'.
Cognitive strategies can be defined in several ways depending on the research area, e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy or education (Nowakowski & Bieling, 2022; Pressley & Levin, 2012).
text.formatted: Cognitive strategies can be defined in several ways depending on the research area, e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy or education <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Nowakowski & Bieling, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Pressley & Levin, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In this thesis, cognitive strategies are defined as mental routines or procedures people consciously use to perform a certain (cognitive) task, following the description of Dijk & Kintsch (1983).

text.text: In case of cognitive dysfunction because of Long COVID, the cognitive strategies people used before their life-changing SARS-CoV-2 infection do not fit their situation anymore; their cognitive capabilities are affected, and so is their cognitive functioning.
This means that if they want to perform certain activities that involve cognitive processing, their cognitive strategies need to be adjusted so they suit their current cognitive functioning.
This can be done by restructuring thinking and reorganizing cognitive processes.

Through changing the procedure to execute a certain task or through extending the procedure through the use of cognitive artifacts 5 , like assistive technology tools, the cognitive functions are complemented such that people can perform (cognitive) activities that they usually cannot do or do not do well (Heersmink, 2015).
text.formatted: Through changing the procedure to execute a certain task or through extending the procedure through the use of cognitive artifacts 5 , like assistive technology tools, the cognitive functions are complemented such that people can perform (cognitive) activities that they usually cannot do or do not do well <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Heersmink, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A common controlled cognitive strategy is the use of epistemic actions.
For people with Long COVID, epistemic actions could play a key role in coping with their brain condition in combination with stimuli and normative standards for daily cognitive functioning.

Epistemic actions rearrange the components of the world that are involved in the action in such a way that the cognitive process is adjusted to a more manageable procedure that is easier to execute (Kirsch & Maglio, 1994).
text.formatted: Epistemic actions rearrange the components of the world that are involved in the action in such a way that the cognitive process is adjusted to a more manageable procedure that is easier to execute <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kirsch & Maglio, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This simplification leads to a reduced cognitive load, which positively contributes to the cognitive capability of a person (e.g., through reduced involved memory, number of steps, and chance of error) (Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Kirsch & Maglio, 1994).
text.formatted: This simplification leads to a reduced cognitive load, which positively contributes to the cognitive capability of a person (e.g., through reduced involved memory, number of steps, and chance of error) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Clark & Chalmers, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kirsch & Maglio, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The adjustments can take place within the internal mind, but also by reorganizing the living and/or task environment, or extending cognitive possibilities with cognitive artifacts.
Through the implementation of cognitive artifacts like assistive technology, cognitive processes can be simplified or at least become more manageable using (artificial) epistemic actions.

This can lead to 1) either a possibility to perform an action that otherwise would have been difficult or impossible; or 2) it reduces mental workload, meaning there is more (cognitive) capacity to perform other, upcoming tasks.

As a result, cognitive artifacts like assistive technologies can enhance the cognitive functioning of people with Long COVID; utilizing epistemic actions, the cognitive functioning capacity is extended, which could also be beneficial for future activities.
Despite the short existence of Long COVID, there have already been developed instructions for selfmanagement strategies.

In a review paper on rehabilitation methods for Long COVID, it was emphasized that cognitive dysfunction should be treated by focusing on developing strategies to rebuild everyday life and improving attention, memory, and executive functions (Gloeckl et al., 2023).

text.text: Another common finding is the use of so-called 'pacing strategies', which are essential to control PEM-related complaints regarding everyday activities.

Pacing teaches people how to manage their condition regarding activities without crashing; by means of experiencing and monitoring symptoms, people develop consciousness of to what extent activities are suitable for them and recognize the need for rest to prevent themselves from worsening their symptoms (Gloeckl et al., 2023; Medinger & Altmann, 2022; Stapleton et al., 2024).

text.text: Lastly, an insightful study by Leggat et al. (2024) on self-management to cope with Long COVID shows that people with Long COVID often develop their own strategies to manage their lives.

text.text: These methods often focus on self-awareness through monitoring, trial-and-error, seeking knowledge, building in pleasure and comfort, and prioritizing the needs of the individual (Leggat et al., 2024).

text.text: It is important to note that self-management methods for Long COVID can be used in rehabilitation and coping with everyday life.
On the one hand, strategies can be used to improve symptoms and rebuild one's life (in case recovery is possible).

On the other hand, self-management methods can enable people to deal with their condition regarding day-to-day activities through, e.g., pacing technologies and extending capabilities using epistemic actions.

Although this thesis focuses on the implementation of technology to manage the cognitive symptoms in executing daily tasks, it is valuable to get some more insight into existing studies about (non-technology-driven) methods that are currently used to manage Long COVID regarding everyday life.
These have several substantial shortcomings, and by acknowledging these, this thesis can prevent them from happening.

Existing research on (self-management) interventions for Long COVID focuses mainly on the effect of the methods on specific symptoms, while this condition is seen as complex because of the involvement of multiple (organ) systems within the body.
Training interventions often only include energy or fatigue management training (Rybkina et al., 2024; Stapleton et al., 2024; Weise et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Training interventions often only include energy or fatigue management training <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rybkina et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Stapleton et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Weise et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: So, these only focus on the symptoms of fatigue, meaning they disregard the complexity and interdependence of Long COVID manifestations.

Besides, these intervention studies often only investigate the impact of the execution or use of these interventions on people's lives, while the exact implementation of (cognitive) strategies and tools like technological devices in daily living processes and environment is missing (Dorronzoro-Zubiete et al., 2024; Stapleton et al., 2024; Weise et al., 2024).

text.text: Knowledge and insight on the actual implementation of cognitive artifacts are essential for further development of interventions, optimization of cognitive strategies, and insight into how cognitive artifacts like technological tools can play a role in the management of the everyday lives and rehabilitation of people with Long COVID.
Therefore, this thesis focuses on how people with Long COVID implement (cognitive) strategies and artifacts.
This thesis takes a human-technology interaction focus on the cognitive self-management of everyday activities for people with Long COVID.

To better understand the (potential) role of technology to support the everyday life of people with Long COVID, it is valuable to look into how people with conditions that result in similar accessibility needs to Long COVID use technology and collect existing knowledge on technology use by people with Long COVID themselvesfoot_1 .

text.text: We can make three observations from (in)formal sources regarding technology use to support the everyday life of people with Long COVID.

1) Technology use among people with Long COVID-related chronic conditions shows the potential of technology as a helpful tool in everyday life; 2) There are only a few technological tools dedicated to Long COVID in particular; and 3) Existing technologies are used by people with Long COVID to support self-management.

Taking a human-technology interaction focus on the topic of supporting everyday life with Long COVID is a logical step; implementing technology in everyday lives to extend (cognitive) capacities in case of impaired characteristics also happens in case of other (chronic) conditions.

We can observe this in the knowledge and experiences of other groups with similar accessibility needs and (cognitive) capacity challenges; many people deviate from the societal or their individual norm because of a (physical, cognitive, or mental) condition on management of daily life could be insightful for people with Long COVID as well.

In the management of other conditions, it is seen that (assistive) technology often plays a role in enabling day-to-day activities (Bigham & Carrington, 2018; Howard et al., 2022; McGowan & Mcgregor, 2023).

text.text: Related work shows the potential of technology in the management of Long COVID in everyday lives; there are multiple examples of academic papers towards the use of technology in other (semi-) chronic conditions like fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue disease, and ADHD that involve Long COVIDrelated symptoms.

Examples of self-management technologies used in chronic conditions are selftracking in Parkinson's disease, migraine, and Multiple Sclerosis (Ayobi, 2020; Mishra et al., 2019; Schroeder et al., 2018), apps to monitor and manage mood for people who suffer from depressionor anxiety-related symptoms (Orcha Health, 2021), and a digital rehabilitation program for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Wienroth et al., 2020).

text.text: You could argue that this reality translates into the development of valid tools for Long COVID; this is lacking as well.
Although there are not many Long COVID-specific tools, it should be noted that initiatives are rising.
There are two examples of Long COVID-specific apps that help you manage your Long COVID symptoms and thus your everyday life.

The (most commonly used and known) apps Fimo Health and Visible record data on the symptoms of their users, which is needed to support them in everyday life by extending knowledge on their condition, and establishing strategies that fit their symptoms (Fimo Health, 2024; VisibleHealth, 2024).

3) Existing technologies are used by people with Long COVID to support self-management.

On the other hand, existing technologies that are designed for another user group than people with Long COVID are often used to manage Long COVID symptoms regarding everyday life (Khondakar & Kaushik, 2023; Orcha Health, 2021).

text.text: This is identified by AbilityNet.

This charity organization that aims to make digital technology accessible for everyone, despite age or disability, provided a list of existing (not specifically for people with Long COVID) technologies that can support people with their Long COVID symptoms.
They divide the tools by symptom type, resulting in technologies to help people with fatigue-and cognition-related symptoms, joint pain, and anxiety and depression (AbilityNet, 2024).

Apart from active self-management during the day using technological tools, people with Long COVID also use existing technologies in another way; they use technology to improve their cognitive (executive) functions through brain training (Katella, 2024).

text.text: From the information on the current topic, we can conclude two points of critique on the current knowledge on the technology use of people with Long COVID to support the cognitive aspects of their everyday lives.

Current technology use in the rehabilitation of Long COVID and managing everyday life is usually not in the form of extending cognitive capacities by cognitive artifacts as described by Heersmink (2015).
text.formatted: Current technology use in the rehabilitation of Long COVID and managing everyday life is usually not in the form of extending cognitive capacities by cognitive artifacts as described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Heersmink (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Mostly, technology in the form of devices, self-tracking, and learning interventions is focused on controlling physical symptoms and complaints or developing cognitive skills such as memory.

Besides, it is seen that current literature about technology use in supporting everyday life with Long COVID is often on the surface; the implementation in the everyday lives of people with Long COVID is missing.

An example of this is the focus on facilitation of regular care through digital solutions instead of integration and implementation of technology to directly support people in their daily activities (Daniels et al., 2024; Hawke et al., 2022; Rinn et al., 2023).

text.text: Another observation is that literature on technology use in the context of Long COVID is often about the potential of wearable devices to track Long COVID-related symptoms through biometrics and the eventual recovery, while insight into the integration in everyday life is missing (Khondakar & Kaushik, 2023; Radin et al., 2024; Stewart et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, Long COVID shuts down the lives of tens of thousands of individuals and causes a high societal burden.
Despite the far-reaching impact, there is no solution for Long COVID yet.
Therefore, the urgency is high to develop management methods for people with Long COVID so they can control their illness better and resume (part of) their lives.

This thesis hopes to contribute to the visibility of Long COVID, gain insight into its impact on everyday lives by giving people with Long COVID a voice, and develop knowledge and ideas on these methods with a human-centered, qualitative approach.
The main research question is: RQ: What is the (potential) role of technology in the management of cognitive aspects of everyday lives of people with Long COVID?
This research question is divided into a few subquestions so that the relevant matters can be included in the eventual answer to the research question.
First, it is crucial to better understand what the impact of Long COVID on people's everyday lives looks like.
As adjustments of cognitive strategies and the use of (technological) tools seem to be crucial in the management of everyday life, considering Long COVID symptoms, this is further investigated.
RQ2: How do people with Long COVID-related fatigue and cognitive dysfunction adjust and implement cognitive strategies and technology in order to manage the cognitive aspects of their everyday life?

To improve the management of Long COVID in everyday life and develop new interventions, it is relevant to look deeper into what is currently missing in the developed cognitive strategies and implemented technologies to be able to carry out daily cognition-involved activities.

RQ3: What do people with Long COVID currently miss in their developed strategies and implemented technological supporting tools to carry out daily cognition-involved activities and what can be improved?
Before answering the research questions, it is important to get more insight into research about people with Long COVID (-related conditions), and suitable research methods for this user group.
Based on these findings, the research method can be developed and eventually executed.
Research into the impact of a condition or a certain intervention on everyday life needs the active involvement of the group of interest in the specific study.
Yet, existing research about selfmanagement interventions lacks recognition of people with Long COVID as the experts.

These studies often focus on new interventions or (para)medical experts' opinions, but do not map the lived experience of people living with Long COVID who developed their own tactics and strategies (Dorronzoro-Zubiete et al., 2024; Rybkina et al., 2024; Stapleton et al., 2024; Weise et al., 2024).

text.text: However, people with Long COVID can be seen as experts in the field; they live with the condition and thus have a unique and valuable insight into how to cope with the complex character of their illness, and have already developed their own strategies and use of (cognitive) tools (Alwan, 2022).

text.text: By ignoring the expertise of people with lived experience and only relying on traditional medical theories, research gets an ableist character (Alwan, 2022; Shew, 2020).

text.text: This still happened in a lot of studies on Long COVID and other post-viral conditions, resulting in a lack of understanding of the condition and stigmatization (Alwan, 2022; Callard & Perego, 2021).

text.text: Therefore, this study aims to listen to people with the lived experience of Long COVID, as to rely on their expertise.
Another crucial factor that should be considered in the study design is Long COVID itself; this condition (partially) disables people, resulting in restricted abilities to participate in studies.

This results in two sets of measures for the study design, namely: 1) minimization of the impact of participation in this study for the participants, and 2) enabling participation despite participants' (potential) disabilities.
It should be noted that these are closely connected.
This research will probably impact the participants because of their vulnerable health.
Our group of interests is impacted by every type of activity, especially the ones that involve cognitive load.

The effect can be, in the worst-case scenario, worsening of Long COVID complaints, like severe fatigue, headaches, and even decline of the disease (this is the case if people suffer from PEM, a common symptom of Long COVID).
This depends on the severity of the disease, the activity pattern, and the specific complaints of the participant.
Therefore, it is important to be aware of the vulnerable health situation of the participants during (the development of) the research method.
It is important that during the design of the research method, the researchers minimize the (cognitive) load as much as possible to reduce the impact of this study as much as possible.
Besides, as people with Long COVID have varying disease profiles, personalization and optimization regarding symptoms need to be possible.

Besides minimizing the impact, the design method itself should also be adjusted to the research group of interest to provide them with the opportunity to be able to participate in the study despite eventually limited capacities.
The research method should complement this goal.
A common method to identify daily experiences and practices is an activity diary.

The benefits of cultural probes like these are that they can be designed for a certain project and user group, the burden for researchers is relatively low, there is room for input, autonomy, and creativity from the participants, etc. (Carter & Mankoff, 2005; Gaver et al., 1999).

text.text: In a paper by Van Rijen (2025), several cultural probe methods in research with people who had a stroke were researched.
The cognitive and physical impairments of people who have had a stroke and people who have Long COVID are partially similar.
Therefore, this paper could be used as a guideline in designing the research methodology.

To empower people to participate in research that is about them, the cultural probe should be adjusted to the needs of the group of interest to make it both useful and reciprocal (Van Rijen et al., 2025).

text.text: This project aims to be participant-friendly.
We are aware of the vulnerable health situation of the participants.
The first researcher of this thesis also has Long COVID for several years and therefore has a good view of the risks and discomforts involved.

Based on her experiences, deductive reasoning, and (in)formal literature, the research method is optimized as best as possible; in this way, people with Long COVID are facilitated to participate in this project and share their expertise with minimal impact on their well-being.

We have tried to minimize the impact of this research as much as possible by adapting the method to the participants' needs, relying on participants' expertise, emphasizing autonomy and (social) safety, and adapting the method to the individual participants' pace.
The following section describes the research methodology that is used to answer the research questions.
>Methodology
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Methodology</head>

text.text: This study is seen as explorative, and (mainly) qualitative.

Using context information about the everyday lives of people with Long COVID, activity diaries, and semi-structured interviews, more insight into the potential role of technology in the management of cognitive aspects of everyday lives of people with Long COVID who experience fatigue-, cognitive dysfunction-, and (eventually) PEMrelated complaints regarding their symptoms and eventual recovery was gained.

The starting point for the methodology was to research this topic in a human-centered manner; the expertise of the participants was leading, and we tried to minimize the impact of this project on the health of participants by adapting the method to the participants' needs, wishes, and challenges.
The study was approved by the HTI Ethical Review Board of the TU/e.
We followed the guidelines for thematic analysis by Braun & Clarke (2013) for the design of the research method, the data collection, and reporting.
text.formatted: We followed the guidelines for thematic analysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Braun & Clarke (2013)</ref> for the design of the research method, the data collection, and reporting.

text.text: Contact with participants for the data collection took place from January 16, 2025, until March 11,2025.

The participants were recruited through snowballing; via informal and formal (social) media such as LinkedIn and WhatsApp, using the (in)direct connections of the researcher(s), potential participants were reached.
The recruitment material can be found in Appendix C.1.
This study focuses on people with everyday life-limiting Long COVID who experience fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and eventual PEM-related complaints.
Therefore, the participants had to experience these symptoms and indicate that the ability to carry out day-to-day activities is reduced significantly compared to before their COVID-19 infection.

Another criterion was the duration of their condition; participants must have had Long COVID, either diagnosed by medical staff or by themselves, for at least half a year following the WHO definition of Long COVIDfoot_3 .
text.formatted: Another criterion was the duration of their condition; participants must have had Long COVID, either diagnosed by medical staff or by themselves, for at least half a year following the WHO definition of Long COVID<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> .

text.text: This ensures that people have had the opportunity to develop management methods and strategies to cope with their condition regarding everyday life.
Besides, participants needed to be aged between 18 and 67 (working age in the Netherlands) to ensure an active, involved life.
Lastly, the study was conducted in Dutch, meaning that participants needed to be able to speak Dutch.

Restricting to one language prevents mistakes, uncertainties, or ambiguities regarding (culturally determined) differences of interpretation of the questions and answers, and the transcription and data analysis are more coherent and transparent.
The initial goal was to recruit ten to fifteen people to participate in the study.
During the data collection, the researchers determined the exact number considering the saturation of the data regarding the quality, depth, and variety.
More than fifteen people contacted the researchers to participate, and eventually, twelve people started participating.
One of them decided to drop out because of the cognitive load of the study design and health complaints.
Thus, in total, eleven individuals were included in the study.
The participants were nine women and two men.
The average age was 51 ranging from 27 to 63 years old.
They experienced long-term complaints caused by a coronavirus infection 30 months ago, at the time of the data collection, ranging from 12 months to 50 months.

Some participants suffered from other conditions, which were diagnosed before developing Long COVID, two got a diagnosis that was (possibly) caused by Long COVID, and others did not suffer from comorbidity.
In Appendix B.2, you can find a more elaborate overview of the participants.
Details in these descriptions were rephrased or left out, and names were replaced.
The first researcher conducted all the interviews and took charge of communication with the individual participants.
She is a female human-technology interaction graduate student at the TU/e who gained experience in qualitative research during her studies.
Although she had no active interview study experience, she did an interview training during her study at the university, and read the book on qualitative research of Braun & Clarke (2013).
text.formatted: Although she had no active interview study experience, she did an interview training during her study at the university, and read the book on qualitative research of <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Braun & Clarke (2013)</ref>.

text.text: During this thesis, the first researcher had Long COVID for more than two (and a half years) manifesting in a range of symptoms, with fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, headaches, and PEM being the most prominent complaints.
This means that she was part of this thesis's group of interest.
This was taken into account and intended to be acted upon in a reflexive and transparent manner throughout the execution and development of this study.
In Appendix B.1, you can find a positionality statement in which this reflexivity was more elaborately illustrated.

The other researchers were (i) an expert in human-centered, qualitative research within cognitive psychology and human-technology interaction, (ii) an expert in dementia-focused human-centered, qualitative research, and (iii) a design expert with experience in (activity) diary methods.
They supported the first researcher with (the preparation of) the data collection and conducted code and theme checks during the data analysis.
Prior to the data collection, insights were gathered to optimize the research methodology.
Firstly, feedback on the data collection was provided by one of the second researchers and an additional design and research expert.
Then, a pilot study with four volunteers, of whom two had similar complaints regarding cognitive dysfunction and fatigue as the group of interest, was conducted.
Besides the materials of the three parts of the study, there was also context material, including the briefing and debriefing, and the informed consent form.
These can be found in Appendix C.2, and Appendix C.3.
The first part of the data collection was a sociodemographic questionnaire.
This aims to collect data providing context about the participating individuals and thus describing the research context.
The sociodemographic questions were both closed and open, ending with an opportunity to broaden the answers with an open field.
These can be found (both in the Dutch and translated English versions) in Appendix C.4.
The form was made available online.
Participants could execute this questionnaire in their own space and time and were asked to fill it in before the first researcher prepared the interview.
For the second part of this study, participants were asked to keep an activity diary for a week.
This method aims to identify daily activities, the workarounds around these, the impact of Long COVID on the everyday lives of people, and the use of technology to support them with their condition.

The activity diaries served two purposes: 1) They provided information on specific use of (the implementation of) cognitive strategies and technological tools which served as preparation data for the -in-depth interviews, and 2) They were used as a probe during the interview provoking responses from the participants in the conversation about the concerned topic as described by (Gaver et al., 1999).

text.text: The activity diary was developed aiming to meet the needs, wishes, and challenges of people with Long COVID to participate in research, as best as possible.

In case participants choose the physical option, they received an envelope by post at their indicated address, including a guideline, fourteen activity diary forms, and pens and markers to be able to fill in the activity diary.
If participants preferred the digital format, they received the forms and guidelines via e-mail in PDF.
The guideline document contained a short explanation of the goal of this part of the study, instructions on the activity diary, and an example of every step of the activity diary.

The activity diary included: 1) A text box in which participants could indicate the date; 2) The day diagram: A diagram in which people could sketch their fatigue, cognitive complaints, mood, and eventual additional health-related complaints over the day using (colored) bars and lines (time in hours on the x-axis, and smileys on the y-axis to indicate the severity/feeling); 3) Boxes around the diagram to describe the activities participants did, with three small boxes to indicate how well the activity went, whether the participant adjusted the activity to their Long COVID complaints, and to indicate the use of technology.
Besides, there were lines to indicate the duration and to elaborate on relevant matters.
They could connect the boxes with the moments in the diagram to indicate when they executed them.
4) The day evaluation: A box to evaluate the day using a 'grade of the day' ('cijfer van de dag' in Dutch) and questions to reflect on the day.
In the day diagram, participants were first asked to report on the course of fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, mood, and eventual other (health-related) matters during the day.

Secondly, they were asked to report on at least two activities that involved (active) cognitive functioning regarding how well the activity went, the duration, whether they adjusted the activity to their Long COVID, the use of technology, and eventual additional comments.
This reporting was done in a text box around the day diagram, which the participants connected with a line to the time it happened.

Lastly, participants could add additional information in the diagram concerning, i.e., the use of technology, stimuli (like cognitive effort, light, and social interaction), rest moments during the day using drawing, words, stickers, or other (creative) ways to express themselves.
The day evaluation was used as an additional way to create insight into how participants dealt with the day (for both the participants themselves and the researchers).
The questions were optional and allowed participants to share some extra thoughts and let them briefly reflect on the day.
The activity diary was executed starting approximately ten to twelve days before the interview.
Participants were asked to report for seven days.
The expectation was that the diary would take 10-25 minutes per day, depending on participants' characteristics and (Long COVID) complaints.

As the expertise and autonomy of people with Long COVID were leading during this study, the researchers did not oblige participants to fill in the form at a certain time in the day but instead let them free.

The activity diary needed to be finished a few days before the interview moment so the first researcher was able to process the information in preparation for the interviews as described by Carter & Mankoff (2005).
text.formatted: The activity diary needed to be finished a few days before the interview moment so the first researcher was able to process the information in preparation for the interviews as described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Carter & Mankoff (2005)</ref>.

text.text: The materials for this second phase of the data collection can be found in Appendix C.5.
The third part of this study was interviewing.
This step aims to complete the data that is needed to answer the research question.
The interviews elaborated on the activity diaries, and the sociodemographic data were taken into account for context.

The principle was to have an open conversation (so not a strict interrogation) about everyday life with Long COVID, focused on the topics of the research questions, dividing the control between the researcher and the participant.
The interview schedule was defined by the first researcher and, with the guidance of the second, more experienced researchers, further developed to ensure quality.
The schedule contains a briefing, a semi-structured questionnaire, and a debriefing.

The list of questions is semi-structured, which means that potential additional questions and suggestions based on, e.g., earlier contact and the activity diary forms were prepared and added to the interview scheme besides the main questions.
Also, these questions were not necessarily asked depending on the input of the concerned participant.

text.text: The original Dutch interview schedule can be found in Appendix C.6.
How The online interviews were conducted via video calls in Microsoft Teams, and the live interviews were recorded with Microsoft Teams.
This software was used in both online and live interview settings to record and transcribe the interview.
As TU/e-students and employees have a secure account, Teams can be seen as a safe platform for research activities.
Nine interviews took place online, and two interviews were conducted at participants' homes.

The interviews could include breaks depending on the individual needs of the participants, and they could eventually be broken into pieces to overcome the barrier of Long COVID-related restrictions to participate in research, as described by Heaton-Shrestha et al. (2022).

(2022)</ref>.

text.text: Another measure that was taken to optimize the involvement of participants was the active proposal to add information via email after the interview if participants felt they had more insights after some time.
The interviews took 36-60 minutes, with an average duration of 50 minutes.
All the interviews were conducted in one take as participants preferred this, and none of them added information after the interview.
After people contacted the researchers about their potential participation, they received a message with dates to plan a call with the researcher for the briefing.
During this call, the researcher briefed the potential participants on the content and course of the study.

This conversation also included discussing preferences (interview date, and choice of activity diary) and the needs (additional adjustments to the study method) of the participant to be able to participate in this study.

After the call, people received an email with the briefing repeated, and they were asked to read the consent form carefully (this can be found in Appendix C.3), sign it, and send it back to the researchers.
After participants gave their consent, had no further questions, and were aware of their rights, the study could begin.
The participants received an email message with a link to the sociodemographic questionnaire and were invited to answer these questions at least two days before the interview took place.
After opening the link, the questionnaire in Microsoft Forms appeared, and participants answered the open and closed questions.
Lastly, they were asked whether they wanted to share anything that was not discussed in the questions.
In case people preferred the physical option, they received an envelope with the activity diary instructions, fourteen forms, and the accompanying materials.
A few days before the activity diary phase started, participants received a reminder via e-mail with a note that they could ask for help with the activity diary if needed.
In the case of the digital option, the activity diary instructions and form were attached to the message.
The next step for participants was to get started with the activity diary.
Starting ten to twelve days before the interview, participants kept this diary for a week.
During this week, the researchers sent a message to the participants to remind them and to offer support.

For each of the days in this period, participants were asked to report on fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, mood, eventually additional (health-related) complaints and reflect on at least two everyday activities that involved cognitive functioning during the day, and eventually evaluate the whole day by a day evaluation.
After participants finished the activity diary for the determined period, they shared their activity diaries with the researcher by emailing them.
The physically filled-in diaries were scanned or photographed.
The researchers sent an acknowledgment of receipt and asked for possible extra pictures in case of unclarity.
Besides, participants were reminded of their interview date and time, and the settled agreements on breaks and adjustments to comfort the participant.
At the start of the interview, the interviewer checked in on the participant, and a short briefing was given by the interviewer.
If the participant had no further questions and agreed with the start of the recording, the researcher started the video and audio recording on Microsoft Teams.
The interviewer followed the interview schedule with additional or adjusted questions, based on the activity diary.
When all the main questions were answered, the interviewer asked whether the participants wanted to add anything to the information they had already shared.
The interviewer informed the participant about the option to share any additions via email when their Long COVID has restricted them too much.
The debriefing was given, the interview was closed, and the recording was stopped.
Participants were told that they could share any additional information afterward via email, phone, or WhatsApp.
The researcher also offered to share the findings at the end of the project (see Appendix F) and to eventually share the published thesis.

text.text: The data analysis consisted of three main components: defining the context of the participants, describing the observations of the submitted activity diaries, and a thematic analysis to answer the research questions.

The context of individual participants was described using the data from the sociodemographic questionnaire, the activity diaries, and the interviews, serving as a definition of the research sample and as background information for (future) researchers.
The aim was to provide insight into the participants' Long COVID stories and background but also protect their privacy.
Therefore, only relevant information was included, potentially recognizable data was described vaguely, and the names were replaced with other names.
The descriptions can be found in Appendix B.2.

Together with the diaries themselves, the notes of the diaries that were made by the first researcher as preparation for the interviews were used to describe how participants handled this part of their participation.
By means of the content, the amount, and depth of the activity diary data, the range and differences between the diaries were described.
Besides, during the interviews, participants were asked about their experiences filling in the activity diary.
These were evaluated using the thematic analysis approach and were discussed.

A thematic analysis was conducted to analyze the lived experience of people with Long COVID, providing in-depth information on the workarounds and use of technological tools in everyday activities that involve cognitive functioning, using the interviews and descriptions of participants.
The instructions of Braun & Clarke (2006 ,2013) on thematic analyses were followed.
text.formatted: The instructions of <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Braun & Clarke (2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">,2013</ref>) on thematic analyses were followed.

text.text: The analysis was performed using the qualitative software program NVivo (Lumivero, 2024).
text.formatted: The analysis was performed using the qualitative software program NVivo <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lumivero, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: After the execution of the interviews, these were individually transcribed by the Teams transcription function and complemented and adjusted by the first researcher, comparing the provided text and audio recording closely.
In this way, the data was transcribed efficiently and thoroughly, while the first researcher also familiarized herself with the data.
During the coding process, the first researcher identified anything of interest and relevance.
This took place during and after the data collection.
The coding was discussed with one of the second researchers, comparing two coded transcripts.
As a third step, the first researcher sorted the codes on a whiteboard, developing patterns, and later on defined the themes (the final version can be found in Appendix E.1).
As this research can be seen as explorative, the themes were based on the data itself (inductive approach).
To increase the quality of data analysis regarding validity and reliability, the themes were discussed with the second researchers who were (partially) familiar with the data.
This also contributed to a broader and diverse perspective on the data.
Based on this input, the themes were adjusted, complemented, and eventually optimized.
As the last step of the data analysis, the final themes were defined and presented in the results section.
In combination with the context information of the participants, these were discussed critically and in-depth using quotes from the participants (translated to English).

text.text: The activity diaries of the participants differed substantially, which complies with the free instructions and differences between personality types.
In this section, the similarities and differences are discussed.
Participants' experiences are shared in the next subsection on the thematic analysis.

The activity diary data differed content-wise; some participants focused especially on cognitive activities while others focused more on everyday tasks that impact the course of the rest of the day, including physical and cognition-involved activities.
It was also seen that some people mentioned their rest moments, the impact of an event on their mood, and the complaints they experienced during or after the activity.
Some substantial differences were observed regarding the amount of information.
The number of activities participants documented differed between one to two activities per day, and information on four to five activities.
Also, the level of detail in the diagram differed; data in some of the diagrams were tracked per hour, while in others, more loosely documented.

It was also seen that some participants included additional features in the diary, like health-related issues in the day diagram, and others indicated their rest moments, use of technology, or other events.
This indicates that participants made the diary their own.
Besides, the depth of the information also differed between the participants.
Some participants elaborated on the activities by providing information on their experiences, feelings, adjustments, or context, or explaining certain choices.
Something similar was observed in the day evaluation.
Another conclusion that can be made from the activity diaries is that the course of complaints, mood, and other condition indicators differs.
For some participants, fatigue and cognitive dysfunction go hand in hand, while others experience a disconnection between these two.
Also, for many participants, mood and health-related complaints seem to be separated from each other.
Besides, in the set of activity diaries, it can be seen that the input of individual participants differed between the days they filled in the diary.
Lastly, it should be noted that one of the participants only documented five days instead of seven days divided over a longer time because of the confronting effect on the participant.
Another participant used her own method as she did not notice that there was a prepared form and guidelines to follow.
The data collection for this thesis was done in Dutch.
Therefore, the quotes were translated into English, referring to the original ones, which are presented in Appendix E.2 with numbers between brackets ([x]) at the end of every quote.
The quotes are translated and paraphrased considering meaning, form, and readability for the sake of the accessibility of the report and authenticity of the quotes.
Details in the quotes that contribute to the recognizability of the participants were rephrased or left out of the original and translated quotes.
The names of participants were replaced by other (random) names, and an overview of them was given in Appendix B.2: Descriptions of the participants.
The thematic analysis resulted in nine themes, of which seven are also subdivided into subthemes.
These themes can be divided into three parts: a) the current situation, 2) coping with the situation, and 3) the use of (technological) tools.
The themes and subthemes are presented based on their category in Figure 3 and further elaborated on in this section.
