text.text: Before introducing the actual themes of this thesis, participants' experiences with the activity diary are discussed in this subsection.
The participants experienced the activity diary part differently.
For some of them, it was cognitively demanding to fill in.
From this, it can be concluded that despite the Long COVID-specific adjustments to the design of the activity diary form, the cognitive load was still experienced as substantial.
Besides, several participants shared that they found it difficult to fill in the form; apart from cognitive load, people seem to have experienced a certain mental load in filling it out correctly.
A few participants explicitly stated that they experienced both cognitive and mental load while filling in their diaries.
Apart from this, people were also positively affected; almost all the participants indicated that the activity diary provided new insights into their Long COVID regarding everyday life.
Especially the impact of activities on participants' health-related complaints became clearer because of the diary, which led to new insights on how to cope with their condition.
Bente explained: "So that's what makes it interesting to consciously reflect on things that take energy.
And that also let me think like how can I prevent that I drain so much on these things?"

text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Some of them also concluded through filling in the diary that they experience that they are doing too many things regarding their condition.
Other participants experienced the diary as confronting because they realized that they are more impacted by Long COVID than they were aware of before filling it in.
An example of this confrontation is Daphne, who has had Long COVID for more than four years but is (partially) actively involved in society.
She stated, "I found this more confronting than expected.

And indeed, you make more adjustments because you do these automatically already, which also felt confronting because I often have the feeling that things are actually going great, and I can do a lot of things, I am doing a lot of things, and I am present with many things.
But that means that I go to bed at 8.30 pm or I am not able to sleep because my head is all over the place.
That is confronting for me." [2].
text.formatted: That is confronting for me." <ref type="bibr">[2]</ref>.

text.text: This also emphasizes the relevance of the activity diary in the research methodology and reflects on the reciprocity of the diary.
It can be concluded that filling in the activity diary was a substantial and intensive process that led to more insight into one's condition and potential strategies for most of the participants.
However, some people also experienced mental and cognitive impact, although it should be noted that that is not per se something negative.
The following themes present how people with Long COVID experience the impact of their condition on everyday life.
This includes how their current situation looks like regarding activities, the manifestation complaints, their social environment, and their mental self-image.
The first theme identifies the experience of all participants that Long COVID prevents people from participating in (cognitive) everyday life.
Because of symptoms and health-related complaints, (cognitive) functioning is impaired.
This leads to difficulties with executing everyday tasks and thus disable involvement and participation in everyday life.
Noortje summarized this impact the following: "Well, you cannot live the life you want to.
I cannot go to work, I cannot go to birthdays, I cannot do any crowded things." [3].
text.formatted: I cannot go to work, I cannot go to birthdays, I cannot do any crowded things." <ref type="bibr">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In certain situations, people's health-related impairments not only lead to difficulties with everyday activities but even result in (cognitive) crashes and errors.
These can be small errors that can also be solved, but they can also be more substantial errors that lead to crashes of (cognitive) functioning.
Cognitive dysfunction can manifest, among others, in difficulties with basic cognitive functioning.
More than half of the participants explicitly indicated that they have difficulties with certain essential cognitive functions that impair their ability to execute everyday tasks.
This includes functions like reading, concentration within an activity, and (forward-)planning.
Besides, almost half of the participants experienced that certain cognitive functions are explicitly impaired because of their Long COVID.
They verified this through measurable/quantifiable activities, such as reasoning capacities through puzzles or language and writing through e-mails.
Basic cognitive functions are essential for functioning well.
This shows that people with Long COVID can experience difficulties with cognitive functioning, which hinder active participation in (societal) everyday life.
This also aligns with the following sub-theme:
Every participant indicated that they find processing stimuli during an everyday activity challenging and can disable one.
As information in any form is involved in all kinds of activities, it is crucial to be able to (actively) handle stimuli.
Otherwise, you are shut down from everyday life.

This pattern is related to several types of stimuli processing; the information within the activity that needs to be processed to execute the activity properly, and stimuli in the environment that complicate the process of the activity.
First, the experiences regarding (relevant) information within everyday tasks are discussed.
Eight participants indicated experiencing difficulties with information processing relevant to the activity.
This means that they are not able to understand the information, that they are not able to convert this into the right action, or both.
This can lead to, for example, difficulties with reading the newspaper or processing traffic while driving.

Especially activities with many steps seem to lead to complications; five participants indicated that they have trouble doing multiple things within or during one specific task, like household chores and personal care.
Veerle explained that this arises for her during her showering process: "It is just really weird, because you would think: what is difficult about showering?
But apparently, I find I very hard.

There are a lot of steps involved; you have to go to the bathroom, you have to take off your clothes in a certain order, you have to go under the shower, the water should have a certain temperature, then you have to think about washing your hair, shampooing, dry off, put your clothes on again." [4].
text.formatted: There are a lot of steps involved; you have to go to the bathroom, you have to take off your clothes in a certain order, you have to go under the shower, the water should have a certain temperature, then you have to think about washing your hair, shampooing, dry off, put your clothes on again." <ref type="bibr">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, this can also lead to difficulties in multi-tasking, which includes multiple separate cognition-involved processing efforts within one activity.
In addition, it should be noted that because of difficulties with processing, filtering relevant information can be tough as well.
Besides, several people experience that disruption of their activity process can be disadvantageous for the activity execution or even harmful for their course of complaints during the day.
This disruption can be caused by small interruptions within an activity.
You could argue that these disruptions within activities can be seen as an additional effort to another activity, which can be associated with multitasking.

Daphne experienced that an everyday activity can be complicated through (external) interruptions: "I have more difficulties with expressing myself in e-mails; when I have a phone call in the meantime, and I came up with a good sentence in my mind before, it is gone, I lost it." [5].
text.formatted: Daphne experienced that an everyday activity can be complicated through (external) interruptions: "I have more difficulties with expressing myself in e-mails; when I have a phone call in the meantime, and I came up with a good sentence in my mind before, it is gone, I lost it." <ref type="bibr">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Besides, deviations in routines are related; deviation from one's regular process increases the cognitive load, which, apparently, is experienced as stressful or leads to errors.
Apart from the information from within the task, people also experience that their functioning is affected by external stimuli, including, e.g., other people, sounds, and decision processes.
Daphne described this for a certain event: "I still find it very unpleasant if I get overwhelmed by crowds.
And if I should enter the room between all these people, and also think where I want to sit, that won't work well.
Then I'll get an error, that just demands too much of me." [6].
text.formatted: Then I'll get an error, that just demands too much of me." <ref type="bibr">[6]</ref>.

text.text: These external stimuli can restrict people from doing certain activities or going to certain events.
Many participants indicated that they experienced having difficulties handling (mental) stress regarding their condition.
They experience that it costs them more to cope with stress.
Roos explained: "If you are in the car and you still have to drive for half an hour, but you have to pee, you experience pressure, stress within your body.
So, it's in the things that lead to unrest in your body which get you tired more quickly." [7].
text.formatted: So, it's in the things that lead to unrest in your body which get you tired more quickly." <ref type="bibr">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Some participants experience a substantial decrease in energy after they have had stress.
It should be noted that even something small can cause stress; it seems that people with Long COVID are triggered and handle stress differently.
As stress and any other kind of pressure are part of everyday life, this finding emphasizes the challenges people with Long COVID can experience regarding everyday life.
This theme demonstrates that participants experienced that health-related factors are interconnected, which contributes to the elusive nature of Long COVID.
If one experiences fatigue or another complaint, this triggers new Long COVID-related complaints (which are not necessarily directly related).
Roos explained: "But if I get cognitively overstimulated, I also notice this in my body. " [8].
text.formatted: Roos explained: "But if I get cognitively overstimulated, I also notice this in my body. <ref type="bibr">" [8]</ref>.

text.text: This is especially observed regarding energy.
After exertion, many participants experienced complaints.
Mismanagement of exertion can be manifested in complaints for a few hours, but also for multiple days afterwards, depending on the level of impact and the individual's condition profile.
Noortje explained how she experienced this pattern: "That Monday, I pushed my limits hard.
Especially the conversation about my little son, which was really necessary, but the day after I was not feeling well at all.
And that Wednesday, it was even worse.
I canceled meetings and I had to lay down in bed all day." [9].
text.formatted: I canceled meetings and I had to lay down in bed all day." <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Besides, energy level, other medical conditions, and sleep quality are associated with complaints and tolerance regarding stimuli.
As Veerle explained: "If I have limited energy, it goes less well cognitively.
I notice this while expressing myself verbally, having a conversation etc.
For example, I am especially bothered by sound." [10].
text.formatted: For example, I am especially bothered by sound." <ref type="bibr">[10]</ref>.

text.text: A significant part of the participants indicated that when they have difficulties with processing stimuli because of fatigue or overstimulation, they can crash.
This sub-theme describes that the insights into complaints differ both between and within people.
It seems that people with Long COVID have developed an understanding of how their bodies react.
For instance, indicated that Henk did not learn anything from the activity diary, as he already has developed an understanding of this illness, as he explained: "I haven't learned anything.
For me it is a recognizable pattern that keeps coming back.
It is going well, so a few things to make it more positive and you have one action that costs a lot of your strength and afterwards everything declines." [11].
text.formatted: It is going well, so a few things to make it more positive and you have one action that costs a lot of your strength and afterwards everything declines." <ref type="bibr">[11]</ref>.

text.text: These ideas are mostly not based on any scientific knowledge, but more on their experiences and observations.
However, some participants experience the manifestation of their Long COVID complaints as unpredictable.
Noortje pointed out this mismatch of one's perception and the manifestation of complaints the following: "Sometimes things feel differently as they are in the end.
So, you think you have more energy than you appear to have." [12].
text.formatted: So, you think you have more energy than you appear to have." <ref type="bibr">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Some experience both an understanding of the course of their condition but cannot always rely on this insight because of the unpredictability of their complaints.
This contributes to the elusive nature of Long COVID in everyday life.
This theme describes that people with Long COVID have different experiences with their social environment.
They appear to have distinct feelings towards the involvement of others in their Long COVID process and their everyday life, differing between and within individuals.
On the one hand, people feel supported by other people, while on the other hand, it can lead to negative feelings.
Therefore, this theme is divided into two sub-themes describing the negative and positive implications of social contact.
Ten of the eleven participants experienced that their social environment can have a negative effect on their energy or mental status.
This can be divided into two categories.
On the one hand, six people experience misunderstanding regarding Long COVID and their specific situation within their social environment.
People experience this as a disconnect between themselves and their social environment.
Some of them explicitly indicated that they are negatively affected by this.
For example, Daphne explained: "Nobody realizes it.
I can still be affected if people ask, 'Does Covid still exist?'
I find that very difficult.
And also, people that say, 'I just go to work, I have been sitting at home long enough now', I find that hard." [13].
text.formatted: And also, people that say, 'I just go to work, I have been sitting at home long enough now', I find that hard." <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Another negative aspect of the social environment can be the impact on one's energy; more than half of the participants experienced that people around them can be seen as energy consumers.
Veerle experiences this, she pointed out: "After people have been gathered together, I am totally drained." [14].
text.formatted: Veerle experiences this, she pointed out: "After people have been gathered together, I am totally drained." <ref type="bibr">[14]</ref>.

text.text: The other side of social contact is that people's social environment serves as mental and practical support regarding their Long COVID.
Especially, the mental impact can be substantial; receiving understanding from people around them is experienced as supportive for their well-being and condition by many participants.
Sharing one's experiences with their condition with others can be mentally helpful, but participants have also found peace of mind in the compassion of others.
Another side of the involvement of one's social environment can be practical support.
Because of supportive coaching and thinking with them, more than half of the participants experience that this practical support of their peers enables certain everyday life activities.
While Maaike executes activities like cooking with her husband, as she remarked: "So we often do it together.
We have a nice cooking island so often I am on one side, and he is on the other side.
My husband is cooking, keeping an eye on it and I am cutting.
So that's how we do it these days." [15].
text.formatted: So that's how we do it these days." <ref type="bibr">[15]</ref>.

text.text: So, practical support can manifest in several ways and can enable one to participate in everyday life.
Also, by taking over tasks or backing up, some participants experienced social support as beneficial.
The presence of another individual can provide a certain type of confidence (by acting as an opt-out version), enabling the person with Long COVID to do a certain activity.

Lastly, more than half of the participants experience that social contact is good for one's mental condition; people get energy from being involved in social contact, which is also beneficial for their overall well-being.
Anouk remarked that her mental battery charges through social contact: "If I have a bad day, I am really bummed out.
But I get a lot of energy from people visiting me or my son, or good weather." [16].
text.formatted: But I get a lot of energy from people visiting me or my son, or good weather." <ref type="bibr">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Because of Long COVID, people experience a change in abilities and energy.
As a result, one's identity has changed, work has reduced, and responsibilities have decreased.
A large majority of the participants experienced a change in their self-image, directly or indirectly.
So, besides the physical effects, Long COVID also impacts the mental aspects of one's self-image.
Noortje described the effect of her health-related complaints on her identity the following: "Your willpower, your passions, everything is gone." [17].
text.formatted: Noortje described the effect of her health-related complaints on her identity the following: "Your willpower, your passions, everything is gone." <ref type="bibr">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Veerle also discussed a similar experience: "I am not sure what happens.
Why you have done your master's, have a really analytical job, but then cannot think that you first need to take off your slippers before you put on your trousers." [18].
text.formatted: Why you have done your master's, have a really analytical job, but then cannot think that you first need to take off your slippers before you put on your trousers." <ref type="bibr">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Besides the change regarding their self-image, participants often looked negatively at their current situation regarding their activities and abilities.
This can be divided into two sub-themes describing the negative feelings towards their current situation and themselves.
This sub-theme describes that some participants think negatively about their current situation.
They experience disappointment and a sense of nostalgia or melancholy towards their life and abilities.
On the one hand, getting Long COVID has felt unfair to some participants.
Some participants stated explicitly that they were upset by their Long COVID, especially during the first period.
While other participants seemed to be more actively disappointed about the things they cannot do anymore because of their condition.

This negative feeling can also be expressed through melancholic feelings towards their (healthy) past as Karin explained: "I did everything on my own at home, odd jobs around the house, the garden, everything.
How could I have ever done it?"

text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Although some people had negative experiences with their current situation, the majority of the participants developed negative feelings towards their current abilities and activities.
This sub-theme describes the fact that most participants think negatively about themselves and seem to condemn themselves.
This especially comes forward in the way people look at their current identity; they feel and/or think that their activities and presence are less worth it.
These feelings can be manifested within activities, as Bente explained about her work: "Because I want it all to succeed, I do not give in to take a ten-minute break doing something else.
I just want to do, like the rest, don't take any breaks and continue." [20].
text.formatted: I just want to do, like the rest, don't take any breaks and continue." <ref type="bibr">[20]</ref>.

text.text: But these can also be experienced regarding the things one does; some participants seem to look down on the activities they do that comply with their needs and desires.
Another comment some participants make is that they choose to do 'lazy'.
Anouk explained: "You look for the easy things, you become complacent.
Almost lazy for some things, but because you have to for many things." [21].
text.formatted: Almost lazy for some things, but because you have to for many things." <ref type="bibr">[21]</ref>.

text.text: This implies that despite being aware that they need to do less because of their condition, they condemn their choices or abilities.
This is also observed among some participants who have the feeling that they should be able to do certain things and experience stress to do good.
You could say that the expectations people and others have towards them do not always match the reality of Long COVID.

Thus, it seems that a lot of the participants (indirectly) condemn their current selves; although they are aware that they are not responsible for their situation and do not have meet certain requirements, they still experience a negative feeling towards the things they are able to do, and who they currently are (because of their condition).
There seems to be a mismatch regarding their ratio and their feelings.
It is important to note that the impact of Long COVID on participants' mental state also manifests in stress responses or complaints.
Some participants experience this when they talk about the topic, for example, during their interview for this study.

Daphne pointed out that she experiences complaints when discussing her condition: "I am noticing, I'm already feeling it now, when talking about it, especially COVID, somehow my breath goes the wrong way.
I am not sure why, but it feels like it is too much indeed." [22].
text.formatted: I am not sure why, but it feels like it is too much indeed." <ref type="bibr">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, Long COVID not only affects the cognitive and physical aspects, but also one's mental state can be impacted.
Although most participants seem to have a (medium) positive mood, they suffer mentally from their condition to some extent.
The upcoming themes describe how people with Long COVID cope with their current situation.
They have developed methods to live their everyday life as best as possible through mental coping mechanisms, trading off desires and needs, and (cognitive) strategies.
Many participants experience that it is crucial to invest in methods to cope with their condition and the associated mental impact.
Therefore, people actively implement mental coping mechanisms to enhance their mental well-being.
A major group of people indicated that accepting one's situation was crucial for recovery and coping with their condition in everyday life.
As Veerle explained: "I just think 'What a nice weekend, I'm feeling very happy.
And I feel awful physically, but I am still able to lie down in my bed.
I have a nice bed, there are only a few things I really have to do so I can take that rest.'
I have come to accept that that's the way it is." [23].
text.formatted: I have come to accept that that's the way it is." <ref type="bibr">[23]</ref>.

text.text: This resignation seems to be fundamental for the mental state of many of the participants and their overall quality of life.
Another mental coping mechanism was to enjoy the (little) things in everyday life.
This does not necessarily come naturally; several participants indicated they actively work on this.
Lotte remarked: "Well, I am actively working on it to not see the glass half-empty but really half-full.
So, I am working hard to enjoy the little things, the things I do have." [24].
text.formatted: So, I am working hard to enjoy the little things, the things I do have." <ref type="bibr">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Some participants also found strength through comparing their health-related situation with stories of people who have more severe Long COVID.
It seems that imagining worse scenarios downgrades the impact of one's own condition.
As a result, they are better able to handle their situation mentally.
To mentally cope with Long COVID, some participants also receive mental support through therapy.
This can be psychological treatment, but also mind-body therapy was mentioned by a participant, and ReAttach therapy.
So, although many participants experience a positive mood, they have to actively implement methods to cope with the mental impact of Long COVID.
It seems to be hard work to stay or become happy living with such a condition.
This theme describes that Long COVID forces people to constantly weigh their desires against their (health-related) boundaries and rest.
This balancing act is a constantly present issue in their everyday life.

Despite their insight into their complaints and the course of their condition, almost all participants experience that it is sometimes necessary to go over their limits to be involved; living and enjoying everyday life force people with Long COVID to cross over their (health-related) boundaries.
Henk also indicated this during the interview: "As I said, I am a bit fatigued because during the weekend I went to a birthday party for a few hours, and I feel that for two to three days afterwards.
But I have that experience, so I knew this was going to happen.
But that doesn't mean that I didn't go to that birthday; I have to participate in social life, otherwise nothing will come of it anymore." [25].
text.formatted: But that doesn't mean that I didn't go to that birthday; I have to participate in social life, otherwise nothing will come of it anymore." <ref type="bibr">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Crossing one's boundaries is often related to efficiency or enjoying activities; people with Long COVID experience that it is sometimes needed to go over their health-related boundaries to do nice things and keep up with the pace of everyday life.
Being involved in experiences outside one's Long COVID bubble often contributes to mental wellbeing, as five participants explicitly mentioned.
Roos remarked: "You make the exceptions for things that make you happy, that produce happy chemicals, and this is one of those." [26].
text.formatted: Roos remarked: "You make the exceptions for things that make you happy, that produce happy chemicals, and this is one of those." <ref type="bibr">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Another pattern that is observed in this theme is that crossing boundaries often takes place in responsibility-related situations; responsibilities that people with Long COVID have do not comply with the needs of their condition.
Noortje explained: "That really wrecked me for about two years.
It has not been good for my recovery, because things have to happen.
Even if I feel really bad, I am still bringing the children away and if I feel even worse, I am still cooking and if it is really too much, I am building marble runs.
Because you have to, my husband works, so a lot comes down to me." [27].
text.formatted: Because you have to, my husband works, so a lot comes down to me." <ref type="bibr">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Besides, some participants indicated that they sometimes choose strategies to handle a certain situation out of comfort, while this is not per se beneficial for their condition.
Thus, participants are often aware of what is good for their condition.

But to participate in everyday life and for their mental well-being, they cross their boundaries; sometimes they choose to do so but, in some cases, situational characteristics determine this for them.
This subtheme describes that all the participants are thinking about implementing rest in their everyday lives to some extent.
So, the concept of rest is always present in everyday life with Long COVID.
Most people indicated that they take rest during the day to survive the day and to be able to do activities.
However, the impact of rest and what rest looks like differed between people and also within individuals.
Some participants do not recover from taking rest as Veerle pointed out: "Besides, I also just discussed this with my husband about resting and restoring.
I have to rest, because I cannot stay up all day.
But when I lie down for half an hour after I have been staying up for some time, I feel energized again." [28].
text.formatted: But when I lie down for half an hour after I have been staying up for some time, I feel energized again." <ref type="bibr">[28]</ref>.

text.text: While for others, a rest moment can restore their energy level.
Others don't want to take rests or have difficulties with taking enough rest moments.
Henk remarked that he does not want to take rest the usual way: "I like to go into nature and walk, because, as I always say, my battery can charge again.
I don't lie down on the couch to sleep, which doesn't work, and I don't want that." [29].
text.formatted: I don't lie down on the couch to sleep, which doesn't work, and I don't want that." <ref type="bibr">[29]</ref>.

text.text: And others, like Wout, are focused on the quality of sleep.
This indicates that everyone is preoccupied with the concept of rest related to their condition; it seems that people experience some kind of pressure regarding resting because of their condition.
Therefore, this sub-theme can be interpreted as advice for future research to look into how people experience (the concept of) rest regarding their condition.

As a result, people with Long COVID cross their boundaries to live their everyday life, but on the other hand, need to consider their health-related complaints, and they need to have some kind of rest during the day.
This act of finding balance between (mental) desires and health-related issues can be related to theme 3 about the trade-off between the negative and positive aspects of social contact.
This theme describes how people with Long COVID adjust their everyday lives regarding their Long COVID.

This includes (practical) adjustments within everyday activities regarding time, stimuli, (cognitive) effort, and capabilities, but also adjustments that contribute to executing cognitive actions within activities.
This sub-theme shows that participants indicated that they adjust their everyday planning regarding their Long COVID complaints and energy.
Some participants distribute activities throughout the day.
But also, more than half of the participants consider (expected) complaints.

For example, Veerle, who adjusted her planning on Mondays because of exertion in the weekends with her children, as she told in the interview: "Also, after the weekend on the Mondays, I never plan anything because I have to take it easy." [30].
text.formatted: For example, Veerle, who adjusted her planning on Mondays because of exertion in the weekends with her children, as she told in the interview: "Also, after the weekend on the Mondays, I never plan anything because I have to take it easy." <ref type="bibr">[30]</ref>.

text.text: And some participants explicitly stated that they plan only a limited number of activities during the day.
Also, structuring everyday life seems to be a way to handle their (health-related) needs.
All the participants recognized that they are not able to execute certain activities without additional strategies; their (cognitive) abilities do not match the original task.
Therefore, they (actively) implement adjustments or tricks to enable themselves to execute (everyday) activities.
These methods are related to minimizing cognitive effort, decreasing the impact of stress, and setting boundaries.
The most indicated solution is to keep activities simple and easy.
But people also implement other tricks so activities, like cooking or meeting with people, comply better with their needs.
A specific strategy is the use of lists or notes.
A significant majority of the participants use lists or notes to support their thought process.

This method is mostly used to extend one's memory; people experience that lists or notes can serve as a reminder tool for everyday details and events like things to do during the day, the content of a conversation with a friend, or groceries.
Lotte explained this the following: "Writing a lot of things down in my diary, also reminders for myself.
And often I also set an alarm.
But especially things people tell you, for example, a friend who goes on a ski holiday in Austria next week.
I write that down, otherwise I just lose it." [31].
text.formatted: I write that down, otherwise I just lose it." <ref type="bibr">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Two participants use lists to structure their thoughts during an activity or to prepare for a certain event.
Bente indicated: "I try to prepare these types of meetings, and I notice that I am a lot in my mind.
So nowadays I write everything down in Notion, what I come up with, to structure everything a bit." [32].
text.formatted: So nowadays I write everything down in Notion, what I come up with, to structure everything a bit." <ref type="bibr">[32]</ref>.

text.text: To recover from Long COVID or event-related complaints (and relapses), many participants indicated that they actively implement strategies and methods for recovery.
This theme has a broad range.
Some people train their cognitive functions, which contributes to their return in everyday life and related activities.
Others did more substantial implementations in their life, like following treatment methods or using medication, which contributes to recovery.
Lastly, nature and walking are experienced by many participants as healing, contributing to recovery.
Wout illustrated this: "So I draw a lot of energy from that during the day and deliberately take rest during the day, walking at a very slow pace, slowly taking your steps.
Not because I cannot handle it physically, but because that rest in pace also provides rest in my head." [33].
text.formatted: Not because I cannot handle it physically, but because that rest in pace also provides rest in my head." <ref type="bibr">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it can be concluded that people with Long COVID actively anticipate their (health-related) complaints and abilities through implementing strategies.
These enable them to execute everyday tasks.
Besides, they are keen to improve their situation through developing and looking for recovery methods and strategies.
The last two themes of the thematic analysis describe the (potential) use of (technological) tools.
This includes the current use to manage or enable everyday life, but also the experiences of desire for technology to support people with Long COVID.
This theme describes that (technological) tools play a role in the management of Long COVID and enable and involve people in everyday life.
However, there are also complaints regarding (the use of) technology in this context.
The current role of technology and tools is divided into two subthemes, and the objections and obstructions regarding technology are presented in a separate subtheme.
Almost all the participants use (technological) tools in the management of their condition to some extent.
Technology is especially used by people to get insight into their condition.

An example of this is Noortje's smartwatch that brings her attention to her physical efforts as she pointed out: "But also without realizing, because you don't feel it that way at that moment, but at a certain point it says: 'you're working out well' And then I'll think 'how?
I wasn't, but thanks'." [34].
text.formatted: I wasn't, but thanks'." <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">[34]</ref>.

text.text: In some of these cases, people experience it to be valuable to adjust their planning or activities in response to the technological output to manage their complaints.
Also, (non-technological) tools to prevent overstimulation are often used to prevent overstimulation.
And in some cases, people have experienced (technological) tools beneficial for the recovery of their condition.
This can also be controlling comorbidity through technology, contributing to the improvement of one's overall condition.

This sub-theme demonstrates the role technology plays in the facilitation of everyday (social) life for people with Long COVID; Technology enables and involves people in (societal) everyday life (activities)
For some people, technology is fundamental in the connection with the external world outside one's Long COVID bubble.
On the one hand, technological interventions can serve as a provider or support for communication between a person with Long COVID and someone else.
Besides, technology can also serve as mental support.
Noortje experiences her Google Home as a provider of social support during her days alone at home, as she explained: "I like it.
I also like that it speaks, then you're feeling less lonely [laughing awkwardly].
It is kind of nice." [35].
text.formatted: It is kind of nice." <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Another aspect of (technological) tools is enabling one to execute activities, through supporting the physical or cognitive aspects.
A majority of the participants use technology to support them with cognitive tasks.
This can be related to supporting information processing, but also other cognition-involved tasks like cooking.
Wout uses adaptive cruise control to support the cognitive aspects of driving as he: "So I don't have to put energy in that to worry about the dynamics of the traffic at that moment.
So, when the traffic slows down in front of me, and the speed decreases below the desired speed from 100 km/h to 90, 80, 70, my car automatically keeps enough distance.
And I have to put less effort and energy into driving." [36].
text.formatted: And I have to put less effort and energy into driving." <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Another use of technological interventions can be to check one's cognitive functioning.
The (technological) tools participants use seem to comply with their needs to get support regarding their complaints.
An example of this is Anouk, who indicated that she has concentration issues resulting in difficulties with writing messages.
She uses an AI tool to check her emails, which complies with her disabilities.
Although many of the participants experience benefits from technology, technology can also be experienced as obstructive.
Especially, a mismatch between the technological intervention and Long COVID is experienced as obstructing.
Maaike experienced this with her smartwatch, she explained: "My watch only drops during the day.
Even if I lie down or do exercises, I have the feeling that I somewhat relax.
But sometimes it can give blue regarding stress, so I am resting, but it does not indicate that I am recharging.
While it feels like a recharging moment for me." [37].
text.formatted: While it feels like a recharging moment for me." <ref type="bibr">[37]</ref>.

text.text: But also, regarding energy management and complaints, phone time, and errors in technology can be experienced as disturbing.
Lastly, Henk indicated that he is not willing to let technology determine his planning.
He explained: "I won't let my watch dictate my life.
For me, it is just to look at how the situation is.
I don't accept that it says that I slept well while still feeling tired.
When I am tired, I do something else; I don't want to be fatigued.
So, I perceive it more as some piece of information saying things are not all that bad, so you can do something." [38].
text.formatted: So, I perceive it more as some piece of information saying things are not all that bad, so you can do something." <ref type="bibr">[38]</ref>.

text.text: It seems that he wants to maintain a certain sense of autonomy in which there is no place for (current) technology.

Half of the people shared the explicit belief that they look forward to technology that supports them in everyday life; they experience a desire to get support (from technology) to comply with their needs.
This emphasizes the potential of technology adoption in everyday life with Long COVID.
Some participants attribute potential to technology in supporting cognition-involved activities.

Veerle shared her view regarding support in information-processing: "If you need, for example, help with something, it would be nice to fill in what your problem is, and it will show you with your video what you should do.
So 'sit down, put your socks off', in a step-by-step plan." [39].
text.formatted: So 'sit down, put your socks off', in a step-by-step plan." <ref type="bibr">[39]</ref>.

text.text: The potential for management of complaints was also recognized by two participants explicitly.
Bente remarked: "If you think about it, you feel yourself getting tired.
But you are not aware of it, not actively.
But if at that moment there would be technology that would perceive this or intervene, saying 'I notice that it is time to do this for five minutes'." [40].
text.formatted: But if at that moment there would be technology that would perceive this or intervene, saying 'I notice that it is time to do this for five minutes'." <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[40]</ref>.

text.text: And some participants experience that current technologies could be improved or adjusted to fit better for Long COVID users.
Noortje explained: "I think regarding Long COVID, the Fitbit can be more specific for this user group.
So not focused on sporting and doing your best, but more on preventing tension." [41].
text.formatted: So not focused on sporting and doing your best, but more on preventing tension." <ref type="bibr">[41]</ref>.

text.text: This thesis explored how people with Long COVID manage their everyday life with a focus on cognitive challenges, and investigated the current and potential role of technology to support these.

The motive was to address the relative lack of insight regarding management methods of Long COVID-related cognitive impairments on the one hand, and, on the other hand, highlight the expertise of people with Long COVID regarding their own condition.
Through three sub-questions, the main research question, "What is the (potential) role of technology in the management of cognitive aspects of everyday lives of people with Long COVID?"
was answered.
This was done using a human-centered, qualitative approach, including a sociodemographic questionnaire, an activity diary, and an in-depth semi-structured interview.

This methodology aimed to minimize the impact on the participant and encourage reciprocity while maximizing the insights into daily routines, self-management strategies, coping mechanisms, and technological support.

The results were nine (main) themes describing the impact of Long COVID on everyday life, coping mechanisms and (cognitive) strategies to manage associated challenges, and the use of technological tools and the potential for support.
In this section, the findings are interpreted and discussed considering the theoretical framework.
This is done through emphasizing three axes among the themes, describing the relevant (underlying) relationsfoot_5 .
text.formatted: This is done through emphasizing three axes among the themes, describing the relevant (underlying) relations<ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">foot_5</ref> .

text.text: After this, the research questions are answered in light of the interpretations.
The third part includes methodological limitations and recommendations for future research methodologies, research, and technology design.
A fundamental underlying interpretation of the findings is the intangibility of management of Long COVID regarding everyday life.
Participants described their condition as elusive, unpredictable, and overwhelming.
Many aspects are controllable (to a certain extent) through the implementation of strategies, planning methods, and coping mechanisms.
The participants indicated that they adjust their daily planning regarding, among others, their activities and length of exertion, considering their capacities and impairments.
However, people with Long COVID also need to act upon the uncertainty of the condition's manifestation and the impact of (unexpected) external factors during the day.
People with Long COVID actively manipulate the input and output of their days, coping with uncertainties and their personal context.
This active role people with Long COVID take in the management of their condition complies with the influential paper of Barlow et al. (2002) on selfmanagement methods.
text.formatted: This active role people with Long COVID take in the management of their condition complies with the influential paper of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Barlow et al. (2002)</ref> on selfmanagement methods.

text.text: According to this view, self-management is the ability of people to manage their symptoms, treatment, physical and psychosocial consequences, and lifestyle changes that are involved in living with a chronic condition.

In order to protect their health-related condition and their quality of life, people need to monitor their condition and adjust their planning regarding cognitive, physical, social, and mental aspects.
Based on the findings, people with Long COVID adhere to these self-management norms.
They constantly adjust their planning based on the insights they gather through monitoring their healthrelated complaints and biometrics through smartwatches.
This is described in, among others, subtheme 7.1.
An example of this is that participants indicated they take a rest after exertion or after (unexpected) stress during the day.
A direct consequence of this is that people with Long COVID are, besides their everyday planning and activities, constantly managing their (mental) expectations.

People with Long COVID take it a step further regarding their self-management as they do not only focus on their health-related condition; they also consider their mental and social desires and challenges.
An example of this is that participants indicated that they sometimes deliberately cross their health-related boundaries to meet these desires; they build in pleasure and comfort.

This complies with the paper by Leggat et al.( 2024), which explains that people with Long COVID implement personal strategies protecting mental and health-related boundaries and needs, and adjusting expectations.
text.formatted: This complies with the paper by <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Leggat et al.( 2024)</ref>, which explains that people with Long COVID implement personal strategies protecting mental and health-related boundaries and needs, and adjusting expectations.

text.text: In practice, they walk a very thin line between all the dimensions involved to optimize their everyday life.
This process can be seen as an extensive control loop.
People with Long COVID try to optimize their day to their expectations, needs, desires, wishes, and responsibilities.
They adjust their daily planning regarding expected complaints and activities, which can be defined as feedforward control.
However, during the day, their health-related condition is affected by the elusive nature of Long COVID and uncontrollable events, e.g., external factors.
Feedback in terms of complaints or warnings from their management devices is used to eventually adjust their planning and control their condition regarding everyday life.

This means that besides the feedforward trade-off of expectations, needs, desires, wishes, and responsibilities regarding their planning, people with Long COVID are in an ongoing negotiation with themselves, deciding what is best at every moment during the day, considering every involved element.

Although participants are not always satisfied with their everyday life, and they cannot always find the optimal path, it can be concluded that they have developed some admirable self-management methods to cope with their complex situation.
They are control engineers working to optimize their everyday life as best as possible through implementing an (almost) all-encompassing control system.
Apart from methods to manage health-related complaints during the day, the findings show that people with Long COVID also implement strategies to facilitate cognitive activities in everyday life.
The participants indicated that they adjust most cognition-involved activities during the day when possible.
These strategies not only serve as a way to minimize cognitive effort and reduce the likelihood of overload but also to manage stress and respect personal limits.
This perspective was, among others, identified in sub-theme 7.2.
These approaches to handling everyday activities can be understood through the lens of epistemic actions as described by Kirsch & Maglio (1994).
text.formatted: These approaches to handling everyday activities can be understood through the lens of epistemic actions as described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kirsch & Maglio (1994)</ref>.

text.text: This fundamental paper presents the concept of reducing the cognitive load of a certain task through simplifying the associated mental computation.
Through manipulating the task environment, the task is easier and thus supports cognitive functioning.
This aligns with the adjustments people with Long COVID deliberately and, sometimes unconsciously, make to facilitate the cognitive process involved in a certain everyday activity.
Through adapting the mental and/or physical environment of a task involving cognitive functioning, e.g., processing stimuli, they actively contribute to a reduction in cognitive load.
Restructuring the task takes place through tactics but also using (technological) tools and strategies as described by the participants.

This also aligns with the concept of extended mind as described by Clark & Chalmers (1998); cognitive functioning not only takes place within the mind but can be extended by external tools and structures.
text.formatted: This also aligns with the concept of extended mind as described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Clark & Chalmers (1998)</ref>; cognitive functioning not only takes place within the mind but can be extended by external tools and structures.

text.text: An example of this is the use of lists and notes.
Participants indicated that they use this as a way to support their memory and reorganize their thinking during an activity.
This means that processing stimuli and memory are (partially) outsourced to tools; the cognitive tasks take (partially) place through a list and the interaction between the list and the individual.

Thus, people with Long COVID actively implement strategies, tools, and technological devices to expand their cognitive capacities through extending the environment in which cognitive functioning takes place.

Existing literature within the theoretical framework showed that most technology used by people with Long COVID is used for self-management regarding monitoring complaints, planning, and training cognitive functioning (AbilityNet, 2024; Katella, 2024; Orcha Health, 2021).
text.formatted: Existing literature within the theoretical framework showed that most technology used by people with Long COVID is used for self-management regarding monitoring complaints, planning, and training cognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(AbilityNet, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Katella, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Orcha Health, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This was also observed in the findings of this study.
Participants indicated to use technology mainly to monitor complaints and eventually adjust planning or activities.
For example, some actively implement feedback from, e.g., their wearables to adjust their planning or activity.
This aligns with research by Khondakar & Kaushik (2023) which describes the potential of wearables as a tool in Long COVID healthcare.

text.text: However, this study shows that this biometric data is mainly used by living experts themselves as input for their self-management methods.
This confirms the potential of wearables in a Long COVID context and shows that it is already used and implemented by people themselves.
This technological feedback and control are mostly physically based.

However, because people adjust their planning and activities, it is not only a way to control physical well-being but also contributes (indirectly) to their cognitive capacities because of complaint management.
On the other hand, the findings show that the cognitive potential of technology is not yet realized.

Although not widespread among participants, it was seen that they all had (even when not directly mentioned) significant difficulties with cognitive activities such as sending letters, answering messages, but also other daily processes, such as cooking or showering, can be tough.
These difficulties and explicitly stated desires for support in cognitive activities, as described in theme 9, show that there is potential for technology.
There seems to be a particular desire for support in processing stimuli within a task.
However, only limited technological support was implemented by participants to facilitate these processes.
The current technological tools that are available do not seem to match this demand.
This complies with existing literature, described in the theoretical framework, on tools regarding cognition.

These mostly include cognitive training to improve one's functioning and treat brain fog as described by studies of ( Florian, 2022; NHS Helath Research Authority, 2023; Research Team BEACON, 2023) or more hands-on/immediate support through time management apps, text-to-speech software, and mood monitoring tools (AbilityNet, 2024; Orcha Health, 2021).

However, the potential for supporting processing stimuli within everyday activities remains.
Despite the strategies people implemented, the difficulties with information-dense and stimuli-intense activities persist.

Based on the extended mind theory of Clark & Chalmers (1998) and Heersmink's (2015) application of this theory, it can be concluded that a cognitive artifact can be of great use. Heersmink (2015) describes how cognitive artifacts such as technological tools can serve as an extension of one's cognitive function.

text.text: As processing stimuli is, despite personal strategies and self-management methods, still a large problem, there is great potential for technology to support this.
Technological tools could facilitate enabling everyday activities which include cognitive functioning.
The potential of technology is also shown in the mismatch between current technology and users' needs and desires.
Some participants experienced that technological tools do not fit their Long COVID-related needs.
This is coherent with prior research on the use of existing technologies that are designed for other conditions or situations (Khondakar & Kaushik, 2023; Orcha Health, 2021).
