text.text: This research shows that this can lead to misunderstanding or misfit in human-technology interaction.
However, despite this mismatch, people still use, among others, their wearables as a support to manage their condition.
Thus, the benefits outweigh the disadvantages.

It seems that adjustments or modules in these accepted technologies are a relatively simple way to support people with Long COVID even better; there is only limited work on work on trust and adoption.
Long COVID is experienced as elusive, unpredictable, and overwhelming.
As a result, it determines completely people's interpretation of everyday life.

This aligns with the first sub-research question, which addresses the impact of Long COVID on everyday life: "How does Long COVID affect the everyday lives of people who experience fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and eventual PEM-related symptoms that severely reduce their ability to carry out day-to-day activities?".
The answer is that Long COVID is all-encompassing.
It impacts people's social, physical, mental, and cognitive functioning and activities substantially.
As a result, people cannot live the life they want or be who they were before their coronavirus infection.
Despite this impact, people with Long COVID have developed and implemented self-management methods and strategies; they take an active role in the facilitation of their everyday life.
People with Long COVID are not bystanders of their condition.
Instead they actively implement methods to manage the related challenges.
This includes managing their health-related situation despite the uncertainties, but also adjusting activities to facilitate cognitive functioning.

This is related to the second sub-question, which focuses on the adjustments people with Long COVID make to execute and be involved in everyday life: "How do people with Long COVID-related fatigue and cognitive dysfunction adjust and implement cognitive strategies and technology in order to manage the cognitive aspects of their everyday life?".

Managing their situation regarding the lens of their desires, needs, and wishes is an ongoing process; they have to constantly adjust their predicted planning, activities, and mental state during the day.
As a result, they cannot rely on any certainties that facilitate 'normal and healthy' everyday life.

This has far-reaching implications for social life, but also physical and cognitive activities, and people's mental state; Long COVID is a constant presence that needs to be considered for every minute of the day.
In practice, this means that people with Long COVID are in an ongoing negotiation with themselves regarding their health-related complaints, desires, and needs regarding activities and planning.
Despite the lack of treatment, people with Long COVID developed their own, personal selfmanagement approaches to cope with their health-related conditions and associated uncertainties.
They monitor their health-related state and condition, both themselves through complaints, and by smartwatches through biometric data.
As a result, they gain insight into their condition and they adjust their planning and activities in real-time, considering expectations, needs, desires, wishes, and responsibilities accordingly.
This active role was also seen regarding cognitive functioning.
People with Long COVID actively implement methods to facilitate their everyday life through extending cognitive functioning.
This is done using epistemic actions, but also the use of strategies and (technological) tools which support cognitive activities that involve, e.g., working memory and processing stimuli.

Thus, these self-management methods, including strategies, coping mechanisms, and (technological) tools do not only facilitate people with Long COVID, enabling them to execute certain activities, but also give them (part of) the lead back in their own story.
They are experts in self-management and actively look for solutions to respond to their challenges in everyday life.
Although all participants have already implemented technology in their everyday lives as part of (cognitive) strategies and self-management, there is much potential for future use.

This aligns with the third research question, which focuses on the potential of technology to support everyday life with Long COVID: "What do people with Long COVID currently miss in their developed strategies and implemented technological supporting tools to carry out daily cognition-involved activities, and what can be improved?".
There is especially a role for extending processing stimuli within cognitioninvolved activities.
These could be implemented in current strategies and coping mechanisms.
Besides, the mismatch between the needs and desires of people with Long COVID and current technologies can be solved.
Adjustments or modules in accepted technologies are a relatively simple way to support people with Long COVID even better, there is only work on trust and adoption.
Although the background and the Long COVID symptoms of the participants were diverse, this study revealed some important similarities.
Despite the diversity in background and health-related complaints, experiences, and strategies of people overlapped (for example, in themes 2 and 6).

Besides, because of the exploratory character of this research, each participant's shared experience can be seen as valuable insight into the (potential) use of technology in everyday life with Long COVID and to generate potential ideas for future work, like technology design (recommendations).
Therefore, this study recommends future research in this field to consider a similar methodological approach regarding participants.
Another discussion point regarding the background is the educational and/or job characteristics of the participants.

The individuals who shared their lived experience were almost all working in mainly cognition-based functions, like a secretary or engineer, in an intellectual environment like a consultancy firm or an educational institution.
However, people with more physically focused jobs are missing.
Their experiences towards, among others, the planning of everyday life, fatigue, rest, and work differ from the research sample.
This means that their self-management of Long COVID and associated experiences probably differ as well.
As this group is a substantial part of society, it is important that they are heard as well.
Although this research tried to reach a diverse group of people, this part of society is missing.
Therefore, it is crucial to involve people from all socioeconomic backgrounds and develop a strategy for this in future research.
Another limitation regarding the research sample is that the people who signed up to participate have noticed the recruitment message in some way and were willing to participate.

This means that they are in contact with their social environment or involved in social media and are open to sharing their experiences; they seem to have an active mindset (or are able to have this mindset).
However, this means that the people who are too ill to go on social media or have lost their social contacts because of their condition were not involved in this project.
So, although this research aimed to make everyday life with Long COVID more visible, there remains a group of people invisible.

Furthermore, this research investigated through the experiences of people with Long COVID how they adjust their everyday life regarding their (health-related) condition using cognitive strategies and (technological) tools.
This was the leading input for answering the research question.

However, a result of this methodology is that crucial insights are missing towards these strategies and tools; it is difficult for people to recognize the adjustments they make because of their condition, because these are deeply embedded in their everyday life.
Therefore, the participants could have seen some examples of how they adjust their everyday activities and planning.
It should be noted that the activity diary already activated thinking about strategies and tools people implement in their lives to support them.
Several participants indicated that filling in the activity diary led to a different view on everyday life and gave them insight into their daily routines and adjustments.
However, there can still be missing crucial insights.
Therefore, it would be valuable for future research to optimize this part of the research methodology towards awareness, so the full scope of tools and strategies would be captured.

A suggestion for this is to visit participants at home to evaluate (potential adjustments in the) living environment and potential present (technological) tools, and observe how they manage certain daily activities.
Resignation and mental state pose an additional research methodological limitation.
This could have led to missing insights into how current strategies and technologies could be improved.
Participants in this research actively worked on accepting their situation and had some sense of resignation towards their condition.
During the data collection, they were asked to think about the things they are missing in their current (self-)management methods.
However, this goes against the welldeveloped mental coping mechanisms of the participants; they try to focus on the positive features of their everyday life instead of the negative elements.
Thus, they protect themselves against the potential negative effects of complaining.
This is an explanation for the lack of information and insights into what is missing in their current (cognitive) strategies and technological tools.
This (potential) protection mechanism was not taken into account during the development of the research methodology.

Although the research method was developed to be as comfortable as possible for the participants, it was not considered how to handle (mental) coping mechanisms that counteract the goal of collecting negatively loaded insights and experiences about everyday life strategies and the use of technology.
This should be considered in future research.
A further methodological limitation concerns the origin of participants' (cognitive) strategies.

Although in some interviews the development of strategies and implementation of (technological) tools was discussed, this research did not focus on where participants' ideas for self-management methods came from.

However, this would have given a good overview of how the care system (including general practitioners, occupational therapists, and physiotherapists) and other information sources play a role in forming these strategies and implementing technological tools.
This could be a good method to map the knowledge and translation gaps.
Besides, these insights would have been an additional explanation for the implementation of these strategies.

Apart from the recommendations that were proposed regarding methodological limitations, there are also some other suggestions regarding future research and design projects about supporting people with Long COVID in everyday life through cognitive strategies and technology.
These recommendations were composed through deductive reasoning based on (the discussion of) the results and limitations of the research.

The research field of Long COVID is young and therefore unexplored, especially regarding the topics of cognitive support and human-technology interaction, meaning that there is an infinite number of matters to investigate and design for.
However, this discussion aims to end with some concrete recommendations for future research and design.
• This research focused on cognitive support through technological tools.
However, theme8.2 shows that technology can also serve as a communication provider and even as mental support through its social features.
Although only a few participants mentioned this social aspect of their human-technology interaction in everyday life, this connection could (potentially) be beneficial for one's mental state.
Therefore, this research suggests looking further into the (social) relation between people with Long COVID and the technological tools they use in everyday life.
Besides, this finding shows that there is a potential for technology to fulfill a role as social support in the lives of people with Long COVID.
This also corresponds to their desires regarding social contact, which are complicated by their (health-related) complaints.

Therefore, it is valuable for designers to look into the idea of technological interventions that can serve as a social companion that complies with the social and health-related needs of people with Long COVID.
• Another suggestion for future research regarding human-technology interaction in the context of the everyday life of people with Long COVID is the adoption of technology.

On the one hand, some participants indicated a mismatch between their own experience and the conclusions of their technological tools (such as heart rate data on wearable devices), but still adjusted their behavior on the tool, while some other participants disregarded this technological input.
Thus, there seems to be a skewed balance of adoption of technological advice; some people follow these insights despite the mismatch, while others want to retain their autonomy.

Therefore, future research should investigate how the adoption of technological tools among people with Long COVID takes place, and how this is related to the mismatches between (subjectively) experienced (health-related) symptoms, and the technological output (which can be seen as an error).

This is especially necessary because of the precarious balance people with Long COVID need to manage in their everyday life, which means that the impact of errors differs from people without Long COVID.
• The discussion of the results concluded that there was a mismatch between the mental state and the ratio of people with Long COVID regarding their identity and experience of productivity.
A potential explanation of this could lie in the cultural standards that, partially, contribute to one's identity.
However, the impact of culture on the mental state is beyond the scope of this study.

Therefore, this study encourages researchers with a sociological, psychosocial, or anthropological background to investigate how mental state regarding Long COVID and other (semi-)chronic conditions is related to cultural standards.
• Current technological tools that play a role in the (self-)management of the everyday life of people with Long COVID are not customized for their condition.
This means that they do not comply with their needs.
This leads to a mismatch between the tool and the user.
Therefore, future technology should be adjusted to the demands of people with Long COVID.
This can imply several things: o Existing tools could be extended with a Long COVID-specific module.
It was seen that, despite the mismatch, many participants use technologies to manage their complaints.
Thus, the current potential of these devices is already optimally used by this group of users.
However, to optimize their use, future design should consider their condition and the associated needs.
For example, by focusing on rest instead of productivity, and implementing certain disclaimers regarding the data about, e.g., the body battery.
o The function of existing tools should be replaced by a Long COVID-specific technological intervention.
This means that a new research and design cycle should be set up in which people with Long COVID are involved from the start to develop fitting technological tools.
Their expertise should be leading, as they are best aware of the needs and desires regarding (cognitive) assistance in everyday life activities.
• Designers of technological assistance tools could investigate how they can support information processing within activities.
One of the participants indicated this as a desire in theme 9.
As people with Long COVID mostly encounter difficulties regarding stimuliprocessing in cognition-involved everyday tasks, there is great potential for technological assistance.
This could be, for example, an AI-involved system that recognizes where the user's process went wrong, advising on how to continue or solve the issue or error.
In this way, the technological intervention is part of the user's cognitive process on the aspects that are not working well enough to handle these activities.
• People with Long COVID have already developed cognitive strategies.
However, designers and researchers could investigate whether these cognitive strategies could be optimized through the use of technological tools.
• Long COVID is a complex condition with multiple (organ) systems within the body involved, leading to several health-related symptoms and disabilities.
Therefore, the needs of people with Long COVID can be seen as an ultimate use case for accessibility in technology.
So, this research encourages designers to actively involve people with Long COVID in the design process, learn from them, and use their expertise as a guideline in their design.

Besides, because of this complexity and manifestation of health-related symptoms, this study and future research and (technology) design in the field of (cognitive) assistance of Long COVID in everyday life can be useful for (research about) the management of other, related, diseases and conditions such as burn-out, ME/CFS, depression, chemo brain, and the consequences of a concussion.
The methodology and the researcher's attitude can serve as a useful perspective for other research on these topics.
This research is one of the first in its field.
It shows that (cognitive) strategies and technological tools can support people with Long COVID in the cognitive aspects of everyday life.

As long as there are no (proven) medical treatments for (the cognitive symptoms of) Long COVID, self-management methods are the only way to lighten the impact of this condition on the everyday lives of people who are living with it.
Besides, there were many things found regarding cognitive strategies and use of technology (that do not per se comply with current literature) because of the expertise of people with Long COVID.
It can be concluded that their input is crucial for the usability of design and truthful research.

Therefore, the researchers of this project strongly encourage other researchers to work further on the topic of cognitive assistance (through technological tools) with the active involvement of people with Long COVID as experts.
Severe and life-limiting Long COVID symptoms have a major impact on the quality of life of people with Long COVID.
Self-management methods are seen as the best option to manage this condition regarding complaints and everyday life.
However, current self-management methods are mainly focused on physical symptoms, while cognitive functioning is crucial for daily activities.

Therefore, this thesis aimed to contribute to more insight into how people with life-limiting Long COVID can be supported in the cognitive aspects of their everyday lives using a technology-focused humancentered approach, investigating the (potential) role of technology.
This was done using a participant-friendly methodology in which people with Long COVID were involved as experts.

In-depth interviews, after filling in a sociodemographic questionnaire and an activity diary, in which eleven people with Long COVID shared their experiences, provided insight towards the impact of Long COVID on everyday life, the current strategies and technology that are implemented to support cognitive aspects of everyday life, and what is currently missing in their (technology-based) self-management methods.

The results show that Long COVID affects all substantial aspects of everyday life; people with Long COVID are impaired regarding everyday activities, involvement in (societal) everyday life, managing their (health-related) condition, social contact, and mental state, and are constantly looking for balance between their complaints, expectations, and personal desires.

Besides, they actively look for solutions to manage everyday life regarding activities and planning towards the challenges that are caused by their condition through implementing strategies and technological tools.
Lastly, it was seen that the role of technology could be taken a step further by optimizing complaint management, considering the Long COVID-specific needs.
Besides, the potential of cognitive support through technology was confirmed by current use and desires regarding technology.
Thus, the answer to the research question "What is the (potential) role of technology in the management of cognitive aspects of everyday lives of people with Long COVID?"
is that currently, technology play a role in the self-management of everyday life with Long COVID, especially regarding (complaint) management and execution of cognition-involved activities.

Future technology could play a substantial role in processing stimuli and, in an optimized form, in complaint management, complying with the needs and desires of the user group, contributing to their quality of life.
This research encourages researchers and designers to actively involve people with Long COVID in future projects as experts.

This study shows that they are solution-focused, have developed several strategies, and implement technological tools to support them with everyday life challenges, and they are aware of their needs and desires regarding (technological) tools.
A prominent aspect to consider is my insider position in the group of interest during this thesis, I have had Long COVID for more than two (and a half) years.

This manifested mainly in 1) fatigue in social, cognitive, and physical aspects; 2) cognitive dysfunction; 3) physical complaints like difficulties in condition, and pain in the head, heart, and muscles; and 4) Post-Exertional Malaise.
My condition had been slowly recovering from severe Long COVID, which was life-limiting, to milder symptoms.
This illness and the recovery process were still going on during this research project.
This personal, direct involvement has both advantages and disadvantages.
My insider position contributes to trust, openness, the feeling of being heard and accepted, and empowerment among the participants.
However, this could also be a confusing role as I am a participant as well; there could exist a conflict between my own experience and the lived experience of participants.
Another potential disadvantage is that participants assume that I understand them and am aware of certain underlying principles, which leads to less information being provided.
Besides, because of the lived experience, I could be led by empathy and understanding, which could affect my critical thinking.
Apart from my position within the population of interest, my sociodemographic background could potentially affect the research process.

The most prominent factor is my culture, in which opinions about recovery and responsibility are seriously intertwined; I grew up in a neo-liberal Western system during a period in which self-sufficiency was heavily endorsed by politics and society.
This concept implies that people are owners of their weaknesses and are responsible for 'repairing' these to comply with a certain norm.
Although personally, I do not adhere to this concept, I am still sensitive to this kind of thinking because of its role in my culture.
This could impact my thinking about how people with Long COVID act upon their impairments and the way they look at (the recovery of) their condition.
As I am aware of this risk, during the data collection and analysis, I constantly evaluated my thinking critically.
Some other sociodemographic characteristics that could influence the research process are my sex and gender, age, and education.
I identify myself as a woman, which could positively affect the participants' feeling of connection, as many of the participants are female; this is an additional insider's position.
Besides, age could also influence the perception of the participants; I am in my mid-twenties, meaning that I am relatively young and thus relatively inexperienced.
This could change participants' attitude towards the research's quality, but also regarding my knowledge.
Another characteristic is my education level.

My academic background can be positive as this could serve as an indication of the importance of researching this topic, and also give me, as the first researcher, the capacity to critically reflect on and recognize patterns in the data.

However, it could also be negative as it could lead to a lack of common ground with participants who have different backgrounds, and it could lead to skepticism regarding participants' viewpoints when these differ from academic sources.
Therefore, during the data collection and analysis, I focused on experiences and differentiated between one's opinion and experience.
During the project, I have taken several measures to minimize potential biases.

The most important one is the active involvement of other researchers in the methodology development, data collection, and data analysis; they critically reflect on my input and check the data analysis.

Other measures I have implemented are thorough literature research to develop the research method and include multiple points of view, keeping a research diary, reflecting on every interview afterward, and critically evaluating potential biases I have.
This is an ongoing process that has led to, among others, new perspectives, adjusted approaches to interviewing and interpreting data, and changes in thinking and actions.
Below are a few examples of this reflexivity during the research process: • One of the participants indicated that (s)he followed a certain therapy, which I am skeptical about.
I recognized my resistance and discussed this with the second researchers.
I changed my attitude to curiosity and focused on how (s)he experienced everyday life with Long COVID during the interview and the data analysis.
• I noticed an additional insider position during conducting the interviews: most of the participants (and the Long COVID population) were women, and I am a female researcher.
Several participants seem to be hypersensitive to this element and emphasized this similarity.
This could have provided confidence to share additional information or experiences they thought were female-related matters, like psychological issues and social constructs.
During the data analysis, this was considered critically.
In the following interviews, I did not expand on these matters from the viewpoint of our shared characteristic.
• During the interviews and phone calls with participants, I experienced how hard it could be at some points to separate my own experiences of living with Long COVID from my researcher's role.
This research is personal as you work together with people with Long COVID and investigate their experiences with the condition.
So, I want to give them a good feeling by confirming their answers and connecting through shared experiences.
After a few interviews, I prepared a few sentences for myself to sustain the researcher role while still maintaining my empathetic attitude.
• Some of the participants compared the current (societal) situation with that before, from their view of living with Long COVID.
They explained that things were going differently when they were young than it is currently going on.
Emphasizing this could be declared by the age differences between us; in these cases, my life experience seemed to positively influence participants' information sharing.

• During the definition of the themes in the data analysis, I noticed having difficulties with reporting certain negative-loaded matters, such as the impact of Long COVID on the lives of people, including a negative self-image.
I wanted to keep a positive perspective and report this.
Besides, by documenting the negative feelings of participants towards themselves and their identity, I would share intimate and complicated information.
I discussed this matter with one of the second researchers, and we came up with a strategy in which we used my own lived experience as a guideline.
For the findings in the intimate and complicated themes, I asked myself how it would feel for me if these would be shared, and based on this, I would conclude whether and how to report on it.
So, my empathy and ethical concerns towards the participants got in the way, but my lived experience could serve as a solution.
• During the data analysis and documentation, I observed that I was projecting my perspective on society towards the explanation for the negative feelings towards one mental state.

Although I did not immerse myself in the topic of culture and societal norms and values on mental self-image, I still developed a certain view on these interconnections through information and opinions from newspapers and podcasts.
I recognized that this was not suitable for this project and therefore focused on the facts, without discussing the findings from a colored viewpoint.

As the relation between culture and identity could influence the (mental) impact of Long COVID, this is briefly noted in the recommendations for future work section in the discussion, and suggested to do future research about this possible relation.
To conclude, I am aware of my socio-demographic background and insider position regarding the group of interest.
These have affected the research methodology, data collection, and data analysis.
The factors that were within my reach have been adjusted to improve the quality of the research.
During the data collection and analysis, I constantly evaluated the process and did active introspection.
Based on this reflection, adjustments regarding methods or findings, or ideas were implemented.
This contributed to the transparency and quality of this thesis.
In this section, the people who participated in this thesis were described.

Based on data from the sociodemographic questionnaire, the first contact during the briefing, the activity diaries, and the interviews, an overview of each participant was created to get an insight into their background.
The names are randomly generated and thus do not correspond with the actual names of the participants.
Anouk is a woman in her early fifties who got COVID-19 in February 2024.

She suffers from fatigue, concentration problems, memory problems, shortness of breath, hypersensitivity to light or sound, muscle weakness, PEM (post-exertional malaise), nausea/reflux, loss of fitness, and dizziness.
Before developing Long COVID, she was diagnosed with allergies, allergic asthma, a leaking heart valve, irritable bowel syndrome, and osteoporosis.
Due to Long COVID, Anouk had to quit her job.
Currently, she is working on a therapeutic basis and coaches a colleague of hers.
She partially lives with her young adult son, who helps her with heavy and practical tasks.
When he is around, she is more likely to get overstimulated because of his presence and interaction.
Besides, her sister and brother assist her with household-related chores, and her friends walk her dog and drive her around.
During this research project, she was starting with so-called 'cogmed' training, which is an intervention program to enhance working memory and concentration.
Bente is a woman in her late twenties with a background in human-technology interaction who got COVID-19 in March 2023.
She suffers from fatigue, concentration problems, memory problems, and headaches.
During her illness process, she recovered partially, but a few months before this research project, she had a relapse, which forced her to start again with recovery.
At the moment of her participation, she had already taken major steps in recovery.
Despite this recovery, Bente is not able to perform her former job and has a different function within the same company.
Her family and boyfriend support her, but she has lost many friends because of her condition.
Her boyfriend does many household-related chores, but she also tries to help him with that, even though she does not have the energy.
They have got a dog which helps her with her planning and physical activities; this leads to a feeling of rest.
Daphne is a woman in her early fifties with a job as secretary of a consultancy company.
She got COVID-19 in December 2020 and since then has suffered from fatigue, concentration problems, memory problems, hypersensitivity to light and sound, headaches, and loss of fitness.
During this process, she partially recovered but also got a few new coronavirus infections, resulting in relapses.
Due to Long COVID, Daphne works less, and the settings have changed into a better-fitting situation.
She is living alone and has a LAT relationship.
Her family, husband, and some friends support her.
However, her social life has changed a lot as she has lost touch with a large part of her social network.
Since she is doing better, she tries to participate again sometimes in social activities, although this does not always suit her condition.
Henk is a man in his early sixties who lives in Germany.
He got COVID-19 in May 2022 and, since then, has suffered from fatigue, concentration problems, memory problems, muscle pain, muscle weakness, sleeping problems, and pain in the arms or legs.
During this process, he experienced ups and downs regarding his complaints.
Before he developed Long COVID, the participant suffered from high blood pressure and tinnitus.
At the time of this project, Henk had contact with a neurologist and psychologist about his Long COVID and sometimes followed a German healthcare program for people with Long COVID.
Henk is not able to work anymore because of his Long COVID.
Because of his age, he does not have any financial issues and thus financial-related worries.
He lives with his wife in a spacious apartment directly next to a park and the mountains.
He experiences that this has helped him during his (recovery) process.
His wife and children support him where needed.
Karin is a woman in her early sixties.

She got COVID-19 in January 2023 and since then has suffered from fatigue, concentration problems, hypersensitivity to light and sound, muscle weakness, loss of fitness, problems with sleeping, shortness of breath, heart palpitations, dizziness, fatigue after, buzzing in the ears, hypersensitivity to television, mobile phone, crowds, and conversations.
Despite her complaints, no medical causes were found in the regular medicine.
Therefore, she looked into alternatives and currently follows the mind and body vision (TMS).
Because of her condition, Karin could not work for almost two years, but the UWV only defined her as partially disabled (for only 5%).
Therefore, she had to start working again and currently works at a library within set restrictions.
She lives in a peaceful neighborhood together with her two adult children and husband.
Because of problems within her relationship, recovery is tough.
In online sessions about the mind and body vision, she finds (mental) support.
Lotte is a woman in her mid-fifties who was a secretary at an educational institution.

In October 2022, she got COVID-19 and, after recovery from this initial illness, she turned back to her former everyday life for a month, but her complaints increased over time, resulting in decreased abilities.
In the end, she had to stop working in March 2023 because of Long COVID.

Since then, she has suffered from fatigue, concentration problems, hypersensitivity to light and sounds, muscle weakness, loss of fitness, problems sleeping, dizziness, PEM (post-exertional malaise), and pain in the arms and legs.
In May 2024, she started taking antidepressants to control her fears and panicking feelings, decrease the intensity of her emotions, and get her nervous system to rest, which helps her.

Her family and friends understand her situation and support her.
At the moment of the research project, she followed ReAttach therapy by her occupational therapist.

She has lived in Spain for two years with her husband and two young children.

{Waarom dit onderzoek?}
Zoals je waarschijnlijk weet, is er nog relatief weinig (betrouwbare) informatie over Long COVID en hoe je hiermee kunt omgaan.
Uit onderzoek dat tot nu toe is uitgevoerd, blijkt dat vooral 'zelfmanagement' effectief kan zijn het controleren van Long COVID-klachten en mogelijk herstel.

Deze onderzoeken en methodes focussen zich vooral op de ondersteuning en controle van fysieke klachten, terwijl de cognitieve aspecten minstens zo belangrijk zijn -en misschien belangrijker-voor het uitvoeren van dagelijkse activiteiten.

Met dit onderzoek wil ik in kaart brengen hoe mensen met Long COVID momenteel omgaan met het cognitieve aspecten van het dagelijks leven en wat er ontbreekt in de ondersteuning om activiteiten met een cognitieve belasting uit te voeren.
Dit doe ik met een technische bril op; technologie kan goed worden ingezet om mensen te ondersteunen in allerhande dagelijkse taken.

In dit onderzoek kijken we dan ook naar welke de rol technologie nu speelt bij mensen met Long COVID in het dagelijks leven en waar technologie potentieel een rol kan spelen om mensen te ondersteunen bij het uitvoeren bij dagelijkse activiteiten die cognitieve belasting vragen.
Veel onderzoek maakt gebruik van kennis van ergotherapeuten, artsen en fysiotherapeuten om de onderzoeksvraag te beantwoorden.

Dit onderzoek vraagt om een andere aanpak; samen met de echte experts, namelijk mensen met Long COVID zelf, wil ik werken aan een antwoord op de vraag wat de (mogelijke) rol van technologie is in de ondersteuning van de cognitieve aspecten van het dagelijks leven met Long COVID.
